PREFACE 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committ ee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One Hundred Twenty F ifth Report of the Committee on Action Taken by 
Government on the Recommendations/ Observations contained in the One Hundred Eighteenth 
Report on Demands for Grants 2020 -21 (Demand No . 4 2) of the Department of Health and 
Family Welfare (Ministry of Health & Family Welfare).  
 
2.  The One Hundred Eighteenth Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and lai d on the Table of 
Lok Sabha on 3rd March, 2020. Action Taken Note of the Ministry on the recommendations 
contained in the Report was received from the Ministry on 12th November, 2020. 
 
3.  The Committee notes that the statement containing the status of imp lementation of the 
recommendations contained in the 118th Report of the Committee has not been laid on the Table 
of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha in pursuance to the direction of Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha. 
 
4.  The Report is divided into two parts. Part- A deals with National Health Mission and Part 
– B with Health Sector containing observations/recommendations made by the Committee in its 
118th Report and action taken by the Government thereon.  
 
5.  The Committee made a total of 48 recommendations relating to National Health Mission 
of 118th Report, out of which 17 recommendations have been accepted by the Ministry and  have 
been enumerated under Chapter I . Chapter II contains 16 recommendations, which the 
Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Ministry’s replies. In Chapter III there are 14 
recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been 
accepted by the Committee and the Committee has made further recommendations thereon . 
While a total number of 1 recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Ministry have not been received, has been categorized under Chapter IV. 
 
(ii)

of 118th Report. Out of th e 41 recommendations, a total number of 7 recommendations have 
been accepted by the Ministry, has been categorized under Chapter I .  Chapter II contains a total

draft Report.

PART – A 
 
NATIONAL HEALTH MISSION (NHM) 
 
CHAPTER - I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
NATIONAL HEALTH MISSION 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.1 The Committee has been gi ven to understand that for most of the States and UTs with 
Legislature (Delhi & Puducherry), the NHM fund sharing pattern is 60:40 between the Central 
Government and the States whereas for Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand 
and North -Eastern St ates including Sikkim the sharing pattern is 90:10. For UTs without 
Legislature, the funding pattern is 100% Central Share. In such a scenario where the Central 
allocation makes for the major budget under NHM, the assumption that the States/UTs, should 
compensate for the reduction in the Central allocation for health is not the right approach. The 
Committee feels that both the Central and State Governments should come forward to share the 
fiscal burden for successful implementation of the Scheme. The Commit tee, however, is also of 
the view that considering the amount of expenditure on health reported by all the States, there is 
a strong need for all the States to increase their health budgets. 
 (Para 4.11 of the 118th Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.2 As envisaged in the National Health Policy (NHP), 2017, both Centre and States should 
strive towards raising government health expenditure to 2.5 % of GDP in a time bound manner. 
Further, as envisaged in NHP 2017 , States should increase their health spending to atleast  8 % 
of their budget and two thirds of such expenditure should be on primary care. While allocation of 
central assistance to States is linked to their development indicators, absorptive capacity, health 
lag and performance in the delivery of health service s, States are also encouraged to mobilize 
their own resources for enhanced Health Budget. As per the Memorandum of Understanding 
(MoU) under NHM, States are required to increase their State’s Health Budget by atleast 10% 
annually. 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.3 The Committee, at the same time, recommends the Department to hand -hold the laggard 
States and find out the underlying reasons for marginal or negative increase in their State 
Health Budgets and take remedial measures accordingly so that the desir ed outcomes on health 
parameters are achieved and the desired level of flow of funds to the different Health Schemes 
especially NHM is ensured. The Committee also recommends the Department to track the health 
expenditure in States on a real time basis. The  Committee hopes that such instances of non -
clearance of pending State share under NHM, as in States of Kerala, Telangana and Arunachal 
Pradesh, are not repeated.  
(Para 4.12) 

3 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.4 The National Health Accounts Estimates produced every year sin ce 2013-14 describe the 
health expenditures and flow of funds by the State and Union Governments.  The actual 
expenditure figures, are however available after a lag of two years. 
 
1.5 Further, the States/UTs are being regularly monitored and all efforts are  made to expedite 
concerned States/UTs for clearance of pending State share. It is also submitted that funds are 
released under NHM to States only on clearance of state share against previous central releases. 
The Ministry has suggested 15th Finance Commission for a Composite Health Index for incentive 
based devolution of funds to States in order to encourage the States to demonstrate performance 
on year on year basis. The 'State Health Budget as a percentage of the total State Budget' (with a 
weightage of 15%) was one of the 11 indicators suggested in the Composite Health Index. In 
addition to above, while releasing the final tranche of release, it is insisted that the State Health 
budget has increased by 10% over last year or the average of last three years. 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.6 The Committee strongly feels that unless all States increase their health budget 
commensurate with the Central transfers, it would be difficult to ensure affordable and equitable 
healthcare in the country. 
(Para 4.13) 
Action Taken 
 
1.7 As envisaged in the National Health Policy (NHP),2017, both Centre and States should 
strive towards raising government health expenditure to 2.5 % of GDP in a time bound manner. 
Further, as envisaged in NHP 2017 , States should increase th eir health spending to atleast 8 % 
of their budget and two thirds of such expenditure should be on primary care. While allocation of 
central assistance to States is linked to their development indicators, absorptive capacity, health 
lag and performance in the delivery of health services, States are also encouraged to mobilize 
their own resources for enhanced Health Budget. As per the Memorandum of Understanding 
(MoU) under NHM, States are required to increase their State’s Health Budget by atleast 10% 
annually. 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
  
1.8 The Committee, taking note of the areas of concern in implementation of this important 
scheme, is of the view that these concerns could be addressed by concerted efforts supported by 
increase in budgetary allocation and adequate human resources. 
  
(Para 4.15) 
Action Taken 
 
1.9 The concerns expressed by the Committee are noted. Regular efforts are being 
made by the Ministry with the Ministry of Finance to increase budgetary allocation for 
health sector. Further, initia tives have been taken to ensure adequate human resources 

4 
 
for efficient implementation of programmes under NHM for providing affordable and 
equitable healthcare.  
UNIVERSAL IMMUNIZATION PROGRAMME (UIP) 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
  
1.10 The Committee appreciates the fact that Universal Immunization Programme i.e. Mission 
Indradhanush has proved to be quite successful. It however, expresses its concern that, as per 
National Family Health Survey -4 data, nearly 47% of India’s poorest children were not fully 
immunised. The Committee notes that the statistics with regard to immunization may improve in 
the NFHS-5 data. The Committee impresses upon the Department not to be complacent over the 
success and recommends that the Department should continue to make all out efforts to make the 
immunization programme hundred percent successful. The Committee hopes that the Department 
would be able to make full utilisation of the budgetary provisions made in 2019 -20 at RE Stage 
as it could utilise only 81.6 percent so far.  
(Para 5.7) 
Action Taken 
 
1.11 The Department appreciates the comments of the Committee and has also noted the 
concerns expressed. Under routine immunization, efforts, are made to vaccinate all children . 
Special immunization drive i.e. Mission Indradhanush  was launched in 2014 with the aim to 
cover partially immunized and left out children and vaccination for pregnant women. The efforts 
are continuing to strengthen routine immunization. Further, Intensified Mission Indradhanush 2.0 
has been undertaken from Dec ember, 2019 to March, 2020 to give boost to the program. The 
Department would further continue to sustain the coverage achieved under Mission 
Indradhanush, by strengthening immunization health system which includes capacity building of 
frontline health wor kers for providing quality services, improving their interpersonal skills to 
address all apprehensions of the parents about vaccines, inter-sectoral convergence for improving 
access and creating awareness, improved micro planning of vaccination sessions, e nsuring 
uninterrupted availability of vaccines and related logistics to the states by real time stock 
management through Electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network (Evin). The utilization of funds of 
Immunization Division for FY 2019-20as on 31.03.2020 was 99.39%of RE (Revised Estimates). 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.12 The Committee also takes note that one of the main reasons for not achieving 100 percent 
immunization particularly in rural areas are apprehensions attached with immunization owing 
to lack of awareness. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry should have 
awareness generation programs regarding the importance of vaccines and develop 
communication toolkits to educate people, especially in the rural areas.  
 
(Para 5.8) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13 Following steps have been taken to create awareness among Beneficiaries about 
importance    of vaccination and other related communication activities: 
 

5 
 
 Awareness generation through electronic and print media like radio spots, television, pos ter, 
hoardings etc.  
 Working on improving inter -personal communication skills and knowledge of frontline 
health workers like Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) and Accredited Social Health Activists 
(ASHAs).  
 Utilizing social media platforms like Twitter, WhatsApp. 
  Utilizing of My Gov platform for IMI 2.0 for creating awareness on the importance of 
immunization.  
 Engaging the Field publicity units of Bureau of Outreach and Communication (BOC) under 
M/o Information & Broadcasting (I&B) for reaching the communiti es and spreading 
information on Mission Indradhanush using folk music and dance, Nukkad Nattak, etc.  
 Social mobilization by Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) and other community 
workers. 
 Incentives to ASHAs for mobilizing the children to the sess ion site and for ensuring full 
immunization to the child at 1,2 and 5 years of age. 
 Delivering free, audio messages bout immunization directly to mobile phones of the 
caregivers from the second trimester of pregnancy until the child is one-year-old.  
 Delivering periodic text messages to caregivers regarding immunization.  
 Advocacy with key political and religious leaders and influencers on the importance of 
vaccination.  
 Advocacy with media to cover positive immunization stories for building trust in 
immunization and vaccines. 
 Mobilizing the private practitioners through advocacy with Indian Academy of Paediatrics 
(IAP)/ Indian Medical Association (IMA) to give out messages on importance of vaccination 
and on the safety and efficacy of the vaccines. 
 Inter sectoral convergence for creation of rumours, myths and misinformation through social 
media including Twitter, Facebook and WhatsApp. 
 
HEALTH SYSTEM STRENGTHENING UNDER NRHM (SUPPORT FROM 
NATIONAL INVESTMENT FUNDS) 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.14 The Comm ittee also recommends that the Department must hold deliberations with 
those States having weakened/poorer health parameters so that they are provided 'additional 
support' for strengthening Health system under NRHM.  
(Para 5.20) 
Action Taken 
 
1.15 Under NHM, the resource envelope of any State/UT is based on socio economic factors, 
health lag and health parameters. The States having weak/poorer health parameters such as 
EAG States, hilly and NE States have been given additional weightage in allocation of 
fun ds in comparison to other States for strengthening healthcare system.  
 
1.16 The Ministry holds regular consultation/interaction with the States at different levels 
and extends both financial and technical support to strengthen health infrastructure and 

6 
 
imp rove delivery of health services. The Ministry has taken several measures in 
consultation with the States to prevent, control and mitigate the impact of COVID -
19pandemic, Additional release  of Rs.1113.21 crore over and above the approved resource 
envelope were made to the States/UTs during 2019 -20 for containment and management of 
COVID -19. Further. funds to the tune of Rs. 4276.68 crore have been released to the 
States/UTs during 2020 -21 under the India COVID -19 Emergency Response and Health 
Systems Pre paredness Package as on 21.09.2020.  
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.17 The Committee is of the view that the scheme of Health and Wellness Centres which aims 
at taking comprehensive Primary Health Care close to the community is a step taken in the right 
direction. It, therefore, recommends that the targets set for transforming these centres must be 
achieved. The Committee also understands that availability of adequate and trained human 
resources at these HWCs is fundamental to effective functioning of the H WCs. The Department 
should also, therefore, lay greater emphasis on integrating Machine Language (ML) and 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) at such centres to provide better screening and diagnosis. 
(Para 5.25) 
Action Taken 
 
1.18 On use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and integrating Machine Language (ML), it may 
be mentioned that AI solutions in Radiology will be implemented in Health and Wellness 
Centres. Further, NHA/PM -JAY is planning to deploy AI/ML technologies for the following 
fields: - 
  
(i)  Disease Di agnosis: AI/ML based standard treatment workflow systems to ensure 
proper treatment and Clinical decision support system with AI/ML based triggers.  
 
(ii) Fraud Prevention: Developing machine learning & artificial intelligence -based 
models for fraud detection and prevention. 
 
REVISED NATIONAL TB CONTROL PROGRAMME (RNTCP) 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.19 The Committee applauds the Government at the launch of the end TB by 2025 – TB 
Harega Desh Jitega initiative but without an increase in the budgetary allocation, the Committee 
apprehends that the program may not achieve the envisaged goal of elimination of TB by 2025. 
The Committee is of the view that since India shares the highest burden of tuberculosis (TB) and 
multidrug-resistant (MDR), there is an urgen t need to intensify the initiatives in this regard. The 
Committee calls upon the Department to ensure that adequate primary healthcare infrastructure 
and trained human resource is available so that the high levels of disease transmission and 
increase in in cidence of drug resistant TB is tackled. The Committee recommends that the 
Department must not let budgetary constraints come in the way of the implementation of this 
programme. The Committee also recommends the Department to take necessary initiatives to 
remove the stigma attached with TB and carry out a National campaign in this regard.  
(Para 5.32) 
 

7 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.20 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has taken following initiatives:- 
 
1. India’s TB Program continues to be one of the largest such pu blic health programmes 
in the world. Introduction of newer drugs, diagnostics and initiatives such as private 
sector engagement and Nikshay Poshan Yojana (Rs 500/ - DBT for nutritional 
support) have been taken to scale. The incidence of TB per 1,00,000 popu lation has 
reduced from 234 in 2012 to 199 in 2018. The mortality due to TB per 1,00,000 
population for India has reduced from 43 in 2012 to 33 in 2018. The Country has 
notified 24.04 lakhs cases during the year 2019, thus reducing the gap in missing 
cases to 2.4 lakhs only. The TB notified cases increased by 12% in the year 2019 
from 21.55 lakhs in the year 2018. 
2. To ensure adequate primary health infrastructure and trained manpower is available, 
the Programme has achieved integration with the general healt h system at all levels. 
TB services have been integrated with Ayushman Bharat’s network of Health and 
Wellness Centres (HWC) as part of Comprehensive Primary Healthcare Services 
(CPHC). The nearly 1.5 lakhs sub centres that will be transformed into HWCs wo uld 
serve as the most peripheral health facility and will be the first point of contact for the 
community to access healthcare. The Community Health Officers are being 
specifically trained on Tuberculosis and performance based incentives have been 
introduced for the HWC. 
3. To address the high transmission of TB in the community, NTEP is expanding TB 
Preventive Therapy (TPT). Effective implementation of TB preventive therapy (TPT) 
would hasten the decline in TB incidence from the present rate of approx. 3% ann ual 
decline in TB incidence to 11%, which is independent of other background 
interventions. Door to door Active Case Finding (ACF) is being conducted for early 
identification of TB cases and initiate them on treatment to break the chain of 
transmission in the community.  
4. For tackling drug resistant TB, the programme has introduced drug susceptibility 
testing for all TB patients at the time of diagnosis itself. With this intervention, in 
2019, 66,255 drug resistant TB patients were detected which is a 14% in crease as 
compared to 2018 (66,255 in 2019 & 58,347 in 2018). Molecular diagnostics have 
been decentralized and a total of 1,264 Cartridge Based Nucleic Acid Amplification 
Test (CBNAAT) machines and 2,206 indigenously developed Truenat machines are 
operational at district level across the country and the programme is transitioning to 
replace sputum microscopy with upfront molecular diagnostics for the diagnosis of 
TB. In 2019, 35.30 lakh molecular tests have been performed which is a 5 times

Observation/Recommendation

AYUSHMAN BHARAT – PMJAY 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
1.37 The Committee believes that there are administrative and implementation related 
loopholes in the Scheme which need to be plugged to make the scheme succes sful. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to develop a fool proof monitoring 
mechanism to ensure no eligible person is denied health care services under the Scheme. There 
is also a need to increase awareness regarding AB -PMJAY among all the  stakeholders, 
especially, the beneficiaries and the empanelled hospitals. 
(Para 10.7) 

12 
 
 
Action Taken 
1.38 (i) A real time monitoring dashboard is available and implementing states provide  therein 
the details of utilization in all districts. Also, periodica l review is held wherever there is apparent 
underutilization or over utilization.   This dashboard provides district level details of various 
indicators such as number of beneficiaries verified, number of hospitals empanelled, number of 
authorised hospital admissions, and number of claims/package wise received and paid.  
(ii) To ensure that no beneficiary is denied healthcare services under AB -PMJAY, a grievance 
redressal mechanism has been developed, according to  which any complaint regarding denial of 
treatment by an empanelled hospital received either through national call center 14555 or on 
grievance redressal portal https://grievance.pmjay.gov.in or https://cgrms.pmjay.gov.in/ or 
through any other medium are immediately assigned to respective State Griev ance Nodal Officer 
designated at each State Health Agency for necessary action. 
(iii) Beneficiary Awareness: A comprehensive media and outreach strategy has been followed to 
spread awareness and empowering the beneficiaries about their entitlements and rig hts under the 
scheme.  This includes use of media vehicles such as outdoor media, digital display at ticket 
counters across various railway stations, announcements at major bus stations, passenger train 
branding, national and regional press coverage, op -eds and advertorials in print media, radio 
campaign, telecast of beneficiary testimonials via Doordarshan, mass messaging through SMS, 
traditional media etc.  Social media platforms such as Twitter, YouTube and Facebook are also 
being utilised. Outreach prog ramme like school contact program, activation programs at village 
level, van campaigns etc. are also being developed. 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.39 The Committee also recommends the Department to evolve a mechanism to address the 
complaints of chargin g fees by the empanelled hospitals despite being entitled under  AB-
PMJAY. 
(Para 10.8) 
 
Action Taken 
1.40 (i) A Central Grievance Redressal Management System (CGRMS) has been developed to 
register, monitor and dispose of grievances under AB-PMJAY transparently and effectively. Any 
aggrieved person can register a grievance on the portal https://grievance.pmjay.gov.in or 
https://cgrms.pmjay.gov.in/. Also, an aggrieved person can register a grievance by calling AB -
PMJAY national call centre 14555. 
(ii) Grievanc e Redressal under AB -PMJAY has a three -tier system at District, State, and 
National Level. District Grievance Redressal Committee is the nodal authority at the district 
level, State Grievance Redressal Committee at the state level and National Grievance Re dressal 
Committee at national level. At each level, there is a dedicated nodal officer. 
 (iii) The AB -PMJAY call centre also make at least two outbound calls to beneficiaries, after 
discharge, who have undertaken treatment. In case, any complaints are raised by the beneficiaries 
related to charging of money or any other issue, the same is considered as Suo moto complaint 
and is registered on grievance portal for further action by the concerned officer. 

13 
 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
1.41 Attention of the Com mittee has also been drawn to suspicious cases where hospitals 
empanelled under AB-PMJAY have carried out fraudulent transactions. The Committee strongly 
recommends the Department to suspend and blacklist such hospitals and take strict action 
against the Hospitals involved in such fraudulent practices. The Committee also feels that there 
is a strong need to monitor the transactions under the Scheme on a  real time basis. The 
Department must also conduct periodic audits and inspections so that the subsidy und er the 
Scheme reaches the needy people. 
(Para 10.9) 
Action Taken 
1.42 (i) For prevention, detection, and deterrence of different kinds of fraud that could occur 
in PMJAY at different stages of its implementation, proactive action has been taken to 
implement comprehensive framework at policy, system and operational levels. 
(ii) Some of the key actions are listed below: 
 All packages prone to fraud are reserved for public hospitals or need mandatory pre -
authorization and require detailed documentation before claims are paid.  
 National Anti-Fraud Unit (NAFU) has been created at National Level. NAFU is supported 
by State Anti-Fraud Units.  
 Beneficiary empowerment is done by system generated messages to each beneficiary at the 
time of – ecard creation, hospitalization and discharge.  
 Feedback is collected through outbound calls and letter after treatment  
 Utilization data is analysed on different triggers and results are shared with States for 
carrying out due diligence 
 Medical audits and Joint medical audits of ho spitals are conducted to identify any 
wrongdoing. 
1.43 In-built checks and balances have been incorporated for preventing fraud and for 
detecting suspect e-cards and transactions based on algorithms.

screening, early detection and referral to an appropriate level institution for treatment. A 
population level initiative for prevention, control and screening for common Non-Communicable 
diseases (NCDs) i.e. diabetes, hypertension and common cancers viz. oral, brea st and cervical 
cancer, has been rolled out in over 215 districts of the country, as a part of comprehensive 
primary healthcare. Screening of common NCDs including three common cancers i.e. oral, 
breast and cervical is also an integral part of service delivery under Ayushman Bharat-Health and 
Wellness Centres. Population based screening helps in mass awareness generation about risk 
factors and early detection of NCDs including common cancers.

20 
 
States, where the share is 90:10) to provide free essential medicines and diagnostic services for

2.29 Cancer is diagnosed and treated at various levels in the health care system. In

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
3.1 The Committee notes that to achieve the set target of 2.5% of GDP at the current health 
expenditure rate, t he total expenditure on Health for the year 2020 -21 should have been 3.67 
lakh crore out of which 1.28 lakh crore should have been contributed by the Central 
Government. A closer look at the past and present health budget allocation clearly defies the 
envisioned health finance objective in National Health Policy 2017. The Committee, therefore, is 
of the view that to ensure that the health spending targets as envisaged in NHP 2017 are 
achieved, the Government has to make consistent efforts to increase its in vestments in public 
health services.  
(Para 3.5) 
 
3.2 At the time when global spending on health is increasing, India has to scale up its 
efforts so that the Indian health sector expands at a much higher rate. The Committee, therefore, 
strongly believes th at the allocations provided for 2020 -21 is not in line with the ambitious 
vision set in NHP 2017. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department 
should approach the Ministry of Finance to provide enhanced allocations for NHM and Health 
Sector in right proportion which would help actualize the objectives of health schemes and also 
facilitate the achievement of targets of expenditure upto 2.5% of GDP by 2025. The Committee 
also recommends the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to expand its pool of resources and 
ensure adequate allocation and optimum utilization of the funds available. 
(Para 3.6) 
 
3.3 The Committee observes that most of the developed economies of the world spend a 
considerable part of their budget in Healthcare. The Commi ttee recognizes the importance of 
human resources in the economic growth and development of a nation and strongly believes that 
improvement in healthcare delivery infrastructure affect income by making human capital more 
productive. The Committee, therefor e, has time and again advocated the increase in the 
Healthcare expenditure of the country. 
(Para 3.8) 
Action Taken 
 
3.4 The Department of Health & Family Welfare has been making efforts to tap other 
resources for increasing public health spending. The budg etary allocation of DoHFW has 
increased from Rs.62,659.12 Cr in 2019 -20 (RE) to Rs.65,011.80 Cr in 2020 -21(BE). In 2018 -
19, Government announced 4% Health & Education Cess in place of 3% Education Cess on 
personal Income Tax and Corporation Tax, to cater t o the education and health needs of the poor 
and rural families.  
 

25 
 
3.5 In addition to the budgetary resources, health education and research has access to Higher 
Education Funding Agency (HEFA). In the General Budget 2020 -21, Government announced 
that the additional 5% cess on import of medical devices will be utilized for financing health 
infrastructure and services in inspirational districts. The Department of Health and Family 
Welfare has also made a proposal to the 15th Finance Commission, for requireme nt of funds for 
strengthening primary healthcare (which includes bridging gap in public healthcare 
infrastructure, addressing healthcare workforce shortage, supporting National Ambulance 
services, support for IT infrastructure and support for essential med icines & diagnostic 
infrastructure), opening new medical  colleges, training of allied health workforce, super 
speciality blocks under Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana, etc. An additional outlay of 
Rs. 15,000.00 crore has been received towards COVID -19 Emergency Response and Health 
Systems Preparedness Package for three years 2020 -24. Further, the Ministry has demanded 
additional funds under Prime Minister’s Atmanirbhar Swasth Bharat Yojna (PM -ASBY) for 
supporting all States/UTs for further augmentin g treatment capacities for critical care for 
emergency response, strengthening of public health infrastructure for pandemic preparedness by 
setting up of infectious disease hospital blocks in all Districts, developing  comprehensive 
diagnostics and treatme nt capacities, strengthening of institutions to deliver Comprehensive 
Primary Health Care and public health interventions in rural and urban areas, to establish state -
of-the-art digital health systems for managing the core digital health data, to support f or research 
on COVID-19 and other infectious diseases, including biomedical research to generate evidence 
to inform short -term and medium term response to COVID -19 like pandemics. However, in 
order to broaden the fiscal space the Ministry will seek additio nal funds during supplementary 
demands as well as RE stage. 
 
Further Recommendation 
  
3.6 The Committee observes that although the budgetary allocation made to Health 
Sector of Department of Health and Family Welfare has been enhanced from Rs.62,659.12 
Crore in 2019-20 (RE) to Rs.65,011.80 Crore in 2020-21(BE), however, the increment is not 
in consonance with the Health Finance goals and objectives under the Health System 
strengthening component as outlined in the National Health Policy 2017. As per the tar get 
set in the National Health Policy 2017 the Central Government has to increase health 
expenditure from the existing 1.15 per cent of GDP to 2.5 per cent by 2025. Keeping in view 
the envisioned expenditure pattern of 35 per cent by the Central Government  and the 65 
per cent by the States, the total expenditure on health for the financial year should have 
been 3.67 lakh crore out of which 1.28 lakh crore should have been allocated to the health 
sector under the Department of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee, therefore, is 
of the considered view that unless and until the enhanced allocation to the Department of 
Health and Family Welfare is not in proportion to the financial targets of the National 
Health Policy 2017, the physical targets and objectiv es of NHM and Health Schemes could 
not be actualised. The Committee, therefore, strongly reiterates its recommendation for 
adequate investment on Healthcare Delivery Infrastructure. 
 
3.7 The Committee would also like to be apprised of appropriation Plan of  Rs. 15000.00 
Crore received towards COVID-19 Emergency Response and Health System Preparedness 
Package for the year 2020 -24. The Committee further desires to be apprised of the 

26 
 
projected demand of the Department under PM’s Atmanirbhar Swasth Bharat Yojna 
(PM-ASBY). 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
3.8 The Committee also takes cognizance of the financial hardships caused by catastrophic 
health illness that drives the population especially the marginalized section to poverty. The 
Committee also believes that India being a welfare state has to make constant efforts to promote 
the economic and social well being of its citizens and make every effort to reduce OOPE. The 
Committee is of the strong view that the aim of the Government must be to provide healthcare 
services as a public good and the State must protect its citizens especially the poor from the 
significant financial hardship caused due to high OOPE. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends the Government to play a major role of facilitator by increasin g the Government 
expenditure on Health.

services. The out of pocket ex penditure is still as high as 62.4 per cent and India ranks 15

is languishing due to its inherent shortcomings viz constricted category of beneficiaries,

was initiated in May, 2018 with a sample size    of   6432 samples taken from 1100 towns with a 
population of over 50,000 across all 29 States and 7 Union Territories for qualitative and 
quantitative analysis. Scope of NMSQS 2018 covered 3 quality parameters (Fat, SNF and water), 
13 common adulterants (vegetable oil/fat, detergents/caustic soda, hydrogen peroxide, sugar, 
glucose, urea, starch, Maltodextrin, boric acid, ammonium sulphate, nitrates, cellulose, and 
neutralizer; and 3 contaminants (antibiotics, pesticides, aflatoxin M1,).   All the 6432 samples 
were collected and analysed qualitatively immediately onsite in mobile vans and nearly 30% of 
those samples that te sted positive for any of the adulterants and/or contaminants were tested 
quantitatively in laboratory to ascertain whether the samples were compliant or non -compliant to 
limits set.    
 
1.16 As per NMSQS final report released in October, 2019 -   
 
- About 7%    samples were found to be unsafe for consumption due to presence of 
harmful contaminants in excess of specified limits coming mainly from poor quality of 
feed, irresponsible use of antibiotics and poor farm practices 
- Only 12 out of total 6432 samples had adulterants that affect the quality of milk 

44 
 
- About 41% of milk samples of the total were, however, non-compliant with reference to 
one or the other quality parameters [fat, Solid not -fat (SNF), sugar and maltodextrin] but 
were without any safety issues.   
 
1.17 Details of survey are  available at   https://www.fssai.gov.in/home.  Thus, the survey 
results indicate clearly that milk being sold in India is largely safe for consumption.   This is 
contrary to the popular perception carried by the consumers owing to misrepresented information 
for various reasons including deceitful campaigns and unsubstantiated reports.  
   
1.18 By regular surveillance, sampling and inspections which are being   monitored through

NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME 
 
Observation/Recommendation  
 
2.20 HIV screening programme and testing programme in India should be in lines with the 
globally accepted best practices and henc e the Committee strongly recommends that NACO 
should consider and adopt the latest non invasive oral saliva testing technology as it shall 
eliminate the apprehensions of social embarrassment besides providing early screening at 
affordable cost. This non in vasive technology would provide an early safer alternative as per 
globally accepted best practices. 
(Para 18.3) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.21 National AIDS Control Programme has a standardized testing strategy with a well 
defined algorithm, wherein an HIV positive t est result is given only after three sequential 
positive results with three different technologies. This ensures that before starting the lifelong 
antiretroviral therapy, HIV positive status of individuals is confirmed. Algorithm for HIV testing 
followed under the programme is placed at Annexure- V. 
  
2.22 Also, counselling has been the backbone of the national programme. In order to eliminate 
the apprehensions of social embarrassment and stigma & discrimination besides providing early 
screening at affordab le cost, counselling of client/ attendee is undertaken before screening and 
after screening. The programme has also adopted Community based Screening and screening by 
lay providers among Targeted populations and ANC population to reach to difficult geograp hies 
and communities. As India continues to harbour a concentrated HIV epidemic among Key 
Population, prevention activities are mainly focused at Key Population, including HIV screening 
and referral for treatment.  
 
2.23 Saliva based non -invasive HIV tests  are basically preliminary screenings as per WHO 
guidelines, exhibiting the longest window periods because concentration of HIV 1 & 2 
antibodies is lower in oral fluids and always need to be followed by confirmatory blood based 
tests at health facilities. The policy of NACP is “Test and Treat” and prior to initiating treatment 

50 
 
for HIV, one needs to confirm that the individual is HIV positive, since treatment for HIV is 
lifelong.  
 
2.24 Globally, non -invasive oral saliva testing technology has not yet replac ed blood based 
HIV testing and no country has switched over to saliva based testing completely. In the past, 
NACP has always been in the forefront by adopting the latest techniques and technologies once 
they are recommended by the global agencies like WHO,  UNICEF, etc and approved for clinical 
use by domestic regulators. Once there is an adequate pool of scientific evidence; such new 
strategies, approaches and solutions are piloted to understand the acceptability and feasibility in 
local settings before they can be considered for adoption under the programme.

NATIONAL HEALTH MISSION (NHM) 
 
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
 The Committee observes that although the budget ary allocation made to Health 
Sector of Department of Health and Family Welfare has been enhanced from Rs.62,659.12 
Crore in 2019-20 (RE) to Rs.65,011.80 Crore in 2020-21(BE), however, the increment is not 
in consonance with the Health Finance goals and ob jectives under the Health System 
strengthening component as outlined in the National Health Policy 2017. As per the target 
set in the National Health Policy 2017 the Central Government has to increase health 
expenditure from the existing 1.15 per cent of GDP to 2.5 per cent by 2025. Keeping in view 
the envisioned expenditure pattern of 35 per cent by the Central Government and the 65 
per cent by the States, the total expenditure on health for the financial year should have 
been 3.67 lakh crore out of which 1.28 lakh crore should have been allocated to the health 
sector under the Department of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee, therefore, is 
of the considered view that unless and until the enhanced allocation to the Department of 
Health and Family Welf are is not in proportion to the financial targets of the National 
Health Policy 2017, the physical targets and objectives of NHM and Health Schemes could 
not be actualised. The Committee, therefore, strongly reiterates its recommendation for 
adequate investment on Healthcare Delivery Infrastructure. 
(Para 3.6) 
 
 The Committee would also like to be apprised of appropriation Plan of Rs. 15000.00 
Crore received towards COVID-19 Emergency Response and Health System Preparedness 
Package for the year 2020 -24. The  Committee further desires to be apprised of the 
projected demand of the Department under PM’s Atmanirbhar Swasth Bharat Yojna 
(PM-ASBY). 
(Para 3.7) 
 
 The Committee takes note of Governments interventions to provide affordable 
healthcare to the common ma sses in the form of free services relating to mental health, 
child birth, adolescent health, family planning, universal immunisation, free drugs and 
diagnostic services initiatives, however, these steps have not yielded the desired results on 
ground level and the common masses run from pillar to post to get better healthcare 
services. The out of pocket expenditure is still as high as 62.4 per cent and India ranks 15 
out of 186 countries in OOPE as percentage of Central Health Expenditure. Although the 
launching of AB-PMJAY is a forward looking programme, however, the programme itself 
is languishing due to its inherent shortcomings viz constricted category of beneficiaries, 
reduction of allocation both at BE and RE stage in 2019 -20, non acceptance/late acceptance 
of the scheme by major States, slow pace of its implementation etc. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its recommendation for the increased Government Expenditure on 
Health so as to reduce OOPE of weaker section of the society.  
(Para 3.10) 

80 
 
 
 
 The Committee is anguished to note a marginal 3.75 per cent hike in the budgetary 
allocation from Rs. 65,011.80 crore in BE 2020 -21 to Rs. 62,659 crore in RE 2019 -20. The 
Department will have to manage Extra Budgetary Resources (EBR) i.e. imposition of 4 per 
cent Health and Education Cess or 5 per cent cess on import of medical devices to be 
utilized for financing health infrastructure and services in aspirational districts. Besides 
that requisite fund would be sought from Higher Education Funding Agency (HEFA).  The 
Committee feels that the ad -hoc and piecemeal arrangements to meet financial 
requirement would not do any long-term good to Health Sector and therefore, recommends 
that Government should evolve a system of planning/arranging seamless and sustainable 
resources.  
(Para 3.15)

umbrella National Health Mission (NHM) at RE Stage 2020 -21 and the actual allocation

crore against the projected demand of Rs. 85158.62 Crore in BE 2020 -21 under umbrella

 The Committee recommends the Ministry to assess the performance of the hospitals

Pradesh, Assam, Goa, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Mizoram, Sikkim have registered 
only single digit increase in percentage terms for Financial Year 2018 -19 as compared to 
2017-18  that must have a bearing on creation of fresh Health Infrastructure and delivery 
of healthcare facilities in these states. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare to urge upon the State Government to enhance 
Budgetary Allocation on the Health Sector so that objectives of the National Health 
Mission are achieved.  
(Para 3.27) 
PULSE POLIO IMMUNIZATION  
 
 The Committee would like to be apprised of the reasons behind non -transferring 
of technology of Sabrin Inactivated Polio Vaccine (SIPV) to any public sector vaccine 
producer in India by WHO despite in principle approval of WHO for transferring of 
technology to one PSU in the country. The Committee desires that the Ministry must go 
into the details of non -transfer of SIPV technology to one Public Sector Undertaking and 
apprise the Committee of the steps taken by the Government in the matter.  
(Para 3.31) 
  
FLEXIBLE POOL FOR COMMUNICABLE DISEASES 
 
 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the allocation of insufficient funds 
for various programmes covered under Flexible Pool for Communicable Dis eases Control 
Programme. The Ministry has already conceded that the lower allocation would affect the 
speedy implementation of kala –azar and Lymphatic Filariasis; and effective control of 
three other VBDs i.e. Dengue, Chikungunya and JE. The Committee und erstands that the 
Ministry would require more funds for procurement/replacement/repairing of Long 
Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLINs) besides the committed liability amounting to Rs. 408.58 
Crore for financial year 2019 -20 towards procurement of LLINs. Addit ional funds will be 
required to implement various strategies of National Strategic Plan for Malaria elimination 
in India by 2030 as laid down in National Malaria Elimination Framework in India 2016 -
2030 and NSP. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommend s that the Ministry of 
Finance must be considerate to the financial requirement of Department of Health and 
Family Welfare for effective and efficient implementation of various schemes  and 
programmes under Flexible Pool for Communicable Diseases.  
(Para 3.36) 
 
UPGRADING AND STRENGTHENING STATES’ DRUG REGULATORY SYSTEM 
 
 The Committee finds as clear cut inconsistency in the statement of the Ministry as 
far as the extended period for this scheme is convened. Whenever the Ministry has now 
considered that this  scheme has been extended upto March, 2021, it had, during the 
examination of Demand for Grants (2020 -21), submitted that an amount to the tune of Rs. 
175.00 Crore was earmarked for financial year 2020-21 and an amount of Rs. 188.00 Crore 

82 
 
could be proposed  in the financial year 2021 -22. The Committee would like to know as to 
which of the statement is true. The Committee feels that the set objective of upgrading and 
strengthening of the State Drug Regulatory System must be achieved through efficient and 
effective implementation of the scheme for the larger public good. The Department, 
therefore, must strive to take appropriate steps in order to achieve the set goals. 
(Para 3.40) 
 
 The Committee is happy to note that in pursuance of its recommendations, the 
Ministry has got a third party evaluation of the scheme conducted. However, it express its 
displeasure over the fact that the Ministry has not responded to its 
recommendations/suggestions to take this scheme further. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department must pay special attention to the States where the Drug 
Regulatory System is faltering and not working at desired level through this scheme.  
(Para 3.43) 
 
TERTIARY CARE PROGRAMME 
 
 The Committee takes note of approval for implementation of District Mental 
Health Programme (DMHP) in 655 districts of the country. The Committee desires that the 
targeted interventions covered under the DMHP must be implemented at the ground level 
so that the observable outcome is reflected. The Committee further  upholds that the 
Department should give equitable impetus to all the components of Tertiary Healthcare 
Programmes and accordingly allocate sufficient budgetary funds to each component of the 
programme. The Committee also recommends the department to conti nue to take 
proactive steps as follow -up action to motivate the State Government to formulate 
proposals/scheme/ strategy on each component of Tertiary Healthcare in order to lay down 
a better healthcare infrastructure in the country so as to ensure global standard healthcare 
delivery at the grass root level. 
(Para 3.46) 
  

83 
 
HEALTH SECTOR (HR) 
  
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION  
 
 The Committee would like to be apprised of actual fund allocated to health sector 
scheme, scheme -wise and institute -wise in response to project ed demand of Rs. 37013.17 
crore in RE 2020-21 along with actual expenditure. The Committee would also like to know 
whether the implementation pace of any scheme/programme under the health sector got 
affected for want of funds.  
(Para 3.3) 
 
 The Committee i s constrained to note that as on 18 th September, 2020 a total 
number of 3876 Utilization Certificates involving Rs. 7513.970 Crore are pending. The 
Programme division concerned of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare must pursue 
regularly with organizatio n/autonomous bodies for submission of UCs without further 
procrastination for early settlement of pending UCs within a set timeframe. 
(Para 3.7) 
 The Committee finds the action taken notes, furnished by the Ministry in response 
to Committee’s recommendations contained in Para 3.9, 3.10 & 3.11 to be quite vague and 
evasive. No convincing reason has been adduced for posts of medical and non -medical 
officers lying vacant under CGHS. The Committee is surprised to find that on the one hand 
there is serious probl em of unemployment amongst Doctors in the Country and on the 
other hand there are posts of doctors lying vacant in CGHS. Had the Ministry worked out 
well in time with UPSC for filling up of vacant posts there would have not been so many 
vacancies. It is eq ually painful that the Ministry is unable to direct its own division i.e. 
Central Health Services for timely posting of specialist doctors in CGHS. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its recommendations as contained in Para 3.11 of 118 th Report 
suggesting the Ministry to identify the appropriate reasons for the shortage of workforce at 
the CGHS wellness centres and take the corrective measure to overcome the same within 
given timeframe so that these centres do not suffer from the shortage of doctors and proper 
healthcare facilities are made available to the beneficiaries. 
(Para 3.12) 
 
SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL AND VARDHMAN MAHAVIR MEDICAL COLLEGE 
(VMMC), NEW DELHI 
 
 The Committee expresses its anguish over the pendency of approval of the 
additional infrastructur e project of VMMC at the revised estimated cost of Rs. 187.60 
Crore since July, 2019. The Committee, therefore, urges the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare to urgently sanction the project so that adequate fund is allocated to VMMC and 
the project is executed at the earliest without incurring additional cost. 
(Para 3.16) 
 
 The Committee finds that an amount to the tune of Rs. 217.00 crore was projected 
in BE 2020 -21 against which a paltry amount of Rs. 30.00 crore were allocated as a result 
of which the  procurement of equipments and machinery was restricted to the allocated 
fund. The Committee is in agreement with the plea of the Department of Health and 

84 
 
Family Welfare about the requirement of additional funds to operationalise vital 
Departments such as Radiotherapy, Radiology, Paediatrics, Medicine, Urology, General 
Surgery, Neuro Surgery by procuring the necessary equipments and machinery to cater 
the patient’s need and care. The Committee, therefore, strongly reiterates its 
recommendations urging the M inistry of Finance to be more considerate in allocating the 
institute, the fund as per the actual requirement, to enable the institute to provide prompt 
healthcare services.  
(Para 3.17) 
 
 The Committee finds that the manpower (Administrative and Para -
Medic/Technician) has been deployed in New Emergency Block (NEB) & Super Speciality 
Block (SSB) on outsourced basis w.e.f. the month of January - February, 2020. The

the de cision to have the Administrative and Para -Medic/Technician on the outsourced 
basis as the system adopted may not generate continuity in the management of the hospital 
due to lack of sense of belongingness, commitment and integrity on the part of the 
employees. The Committee, recommends the Department to fill up the sanctioned post of 
technical manpower on regular basis. 
(Para 3.20) 
 
 The Committee has been given to understand that funds required for construction 
of Dwarka Residential Complex for Nurses was not allocated in BE 2020-21 and, therefore, 
the Ministry was forced to place its supplementary demand. The Committee would like to 
know whether the supplementary demand of the Ministry for the Construction of Dwarka 
Residential Complex was accorded and if  so, whether the construction project has been 
started at the ground level. The Committee further feels that once the additional 
infrastructure project for VMMC at the cost of Rs. 187.60 Crores get the approval of the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare,  the Ministry of Finance would allocate adequate 
fund to the said project is provisioned for construction of additional lecture theatre, hostels 
for students and recreational facilities. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends 
the Department of Healt h and Family Welfare to assess and approve the project and 
pursue with the Ministry of Finance to allocate the additional fund without further delay so 
that the proposed project is completed without time and cost overruns. 
(Para 3.23) 
 
DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHIA HOSPITAL 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern that the Department of Health and Family 
Welfare is making lame excuses for non -optimal utilization of allocated fund to RML 
Hospital and RML PGIMER and making untenable plea by calling them genuine reasons.  
The Committee had observed that in the year 2019 -20 the actual expenditure for Dr. Ram 
Manohar Lohia Hospital has been Rs 547.74 crore up to 17.01.2020 against allocation of 
Rs. 744.88 crore at RE stage. The actual expenditure for Dr. RML PGIMER, New Delh i 
has been Rs. 58.11 crore out of allocation of Rs. 138.57 crore at RE stage. The Committee 
has been given to understand that fund allocated under the capital head has been 
insufficient. However, actual capital expenditure in the year 2019 -2020 (up to 17.0 1.2020) 
has been far below the allocated amount. Responding to that, the Ministry took the plea of 

85 
 
various genuine reasons that included non filling up of various vacant posts, non -receipt of 
bills from vendor for payment of Bonus, late receipt of RE 2019 -20, non-placing of orders 
on GeM (Government-e-Market) due to lockdown etc. in the aftermath of COVID -19. The 
Committee, understands that the said  lockdown was imposed on 25 th March, 2020 and 
hence could not be the possible reason for underutilization of a llocated funds. The 
Committee feels that the Department could have taken adequate steps for better co -
ordination and exercise financial prudence for ensuring optimal utilization of fund 
earmarked especially under capital head which is the hallmark for developmental projects.  
 
(Para 3.27) 
VACANCY POSITION AT RML HOSPITAL 
 
 The Committee is well aware that recruitment of manpower is an ongoing process 
but it feels that had the Department adhered to the said principles of HRM and 
implemented the same on regul ar interval there would have not been backlog of filling up 
of 1119 posts, that are lying vacant in RML Hospital. The Committee cautions that all is 
not well with Dr. RML Hospital. It would not be unreasonable and inappropriate to 
conclude that plea on the  part of the Department that continuous efforts were made to fill 
up the vacant posts does not hold ground. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends 
the Department to expedite the process of filling up of the 1119 vacant posts without 
further delay. T he Committee desires that the proposed revival of 486 posts, which were 
kept in abolished category, may be taken up on priority basis. The Committee also 
recommends that the cadre review proposal of administrative staff of Dr. RML Hospital 
must be finalized to streamline the administrative cadre both at higher as well as mid level. 
The Committee believes that the constitution of recruitment cell in Dr. RML Hospital 
would smoothen the recruitment process and prove effective in filling up of regular vacant 
posts under the supervision of Recruitment Committee and Question Paper Committee.  
(Para 3.32) 
 
LADY HARDING MEDICAL COLLEGE (LHMC) & SMT. S.K. HOSPITAL 
 
 The Committee is deeply anguished to observe that the Department of Health and 
Family welfare is furnishing ambiguous and cryptic Action Taken Notes entailing its efforts 
made in the year 2017, 2018 and 2019 in response to the Committee’s recommendations 
contained in Para 6.3 and 6.4 of 118 th Report, that was presented to the Parliament on 
3rdMarch, 2020. The Committee formulated its recommendations based on the facts 
submitted by the Department about the vacancy position in LHMC & SSKH as on 31 st 
December, 2019. On that date, 883 posts were lying vacant against the sanctioned strength 
of 2117 posts thus th e vacancy constituting 40% of total sanctioned strength. Out of total 
strength of 2117 posts, the 71 posts (03 in Group – C and 68 in Group – D) have now been 
abolished, therefore, the total sanctioned strength reduced to 2046. Against that total 
sanctioned strength of 2046 posts, the in-position strength remains 1278 and vacancy of 768 
posts still persists. The Committee understands that Outbreak of Pandemic COVID -19 
could have slowed down the recruitment process, however, the Committee feels that the 
Department could have furnished the convincing response to its recommendations. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that the Department of Health and 
Family Welfare need to set up a definite timeframe to complete the recruitment process so 

86 
 
as to fill up all the vacancies in LHMC & SSKH without much delay. That would not only 
relieve the overburdened existing staff due to heavy patient load but also help the suffering 
patient to avail better healthcare facilities.  
(Para 3.39) 
 
PRADHAN MANTRI SWASTHYA YOJANA (PMSSY) :- POOR FACULTY STATUS 
 
 The Committee is not satisfied with the pace of recruitment process in First Six 
AIIMS under PMSSY as the status of vacancy marginally improved over a period of more 
than eight months. During the course of examination of Demand for Grants (2020 -21), the 
Committee was apprised that against the sanctioned strength of 1830 posts, 1035 posts were 
filled up, thus indicating 56.56% of the total sanctioned strength. As on 30 th Septemeber, 
2020 against the sanctione d strength of 1830 posts, 1092 posts have been filled up thus 
reflecting in position strength of 59.67% of the total sanctioned strength. The Committee 
understands that a huge gap of 44.44 % in the workforce would certainly hinder the 
delivery of quality h ealthcare as expected from a Centre of Par Excellence hospitals of 
national importance. The Committee takes into account the detailed steps/efforts made by 
the Government to improve the faculty and non -faculty posts in First Six AIIMS, however, 
the outcome is not very encouraging. The Committee is of the considered opinion that the 
gap in the workforce in the First Six AIIMS would deter the achievement of long term 
vision of transforming these institutions as centre of excellence in the field of tertiary 
healthcare, medical education and research leaving apart the envisioned objective of 
assuming leadership roles and projecting as role models in their respective regions. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation to fill up the vacant posts, soo ner the 
better, though, without compromising the matching standards in the faculty selection so as 
to be extolled as hospitals of national importance.  
(Para 3.45) 
PMSSY: VACANCY POSITION OF NON-FACULTY STAFF 
 
 The Committee expresses its deep anguish over  the snail’s pace at which the 
recruitment process of non faculty posts in First Six AIIMS under PMSSY is going on. The 
Committee observes that against the sanctioned strength of 22,656 non -faculty posts, only 
11,606 posts remain filled up thus indicating 51.22% of filled up posts against the total 
sanctioned strength. In view of the paramount role that non -faculty staff play in successful 
management of various Departments of the institute of national importance, the Committee 
recommends the Department of H ealth and Family Welfare to regularly monitor the 
recruitment process of non -faculty staff in the first six AIIMS of the country that are 
supposed to play pivotal role for laying the path for other regional AIIMS. The Committee 
believes that the envisaged uniformity in the Recruitment Rules for non -faculty posts 
across all AIIMS followed by Common Recruitment Process would accelerate the 
streamlining of Common Recruitment Process for all six AIIMS and thus filling up of all 
the non-faculty posts without further procrastination. 
(Para 3.48)

A patient who is clinically symptomatic and suspected to have an AIDS indicator
condition/disease is referred to the SA-ICTC for confirmation of the diagnosis. ln this case,
the same blood sample is tested twice using kits with either different antigens or principles.
The patient is declared H|V-negative if the first test is non-reactive and as H|V-positive
when both tests show reactive results. When there is discordance behveen the first two
tests (first reactive and the second non-reactive), a third test is done. When the third test is
also negative it is reported as negative. When the third test is reactive, it is reported as
indeterminate and the individual is retested after 14-28 days.

so as to address the shortage offaculty and Non-faculty posts :
A. MotIFW have issued appropriate guidelines in the matter of recruitment to various posts created for the
institutes from time to time and are applicable to all the AIIMS as below:
(i) The provision has been made in the AIIMS Act for the constitution of Standing Selection Committees.

fixed period: The individual Institutes may consider downgrading of posts with the approval ofGoverning
Body, in the eventuality of difficulties in filling up of the posts, as per decision given by CIB against Iteri
No.4/5 (Para-5) of the minutes of the meeting held on 27tt luly,Z0l9.
(b) Running advertisement with one-year validity for recruitment of faculty: In the one year running
advertisement, short advertisement or website notices may be issued several times as may be required,
depending upon actual progress of recruitment, with clear mention of cut off dates for submission of
application and eligibiliry, each rime.
(iv) Temporary diversion of posts from one Department to another Department for Contractual appointment to meet
urgent requirement of faculty ofa Department.

AIIMS Regulations notified vide Notification No. l4-3l69(98)/Coordination Cell PartJI dated 18.10.2019
(Regulation l2). The Combined Selection Committees and Regional Selection Committees may undertake
common selection for various faculty positions for more than one or for all AIIMS.
(iii) In case offaculty recruitment, provisions have been made for:
(v) Relaxation of essential teaching/research experience up to a period of one year to SC/ST candidates under the
guidelines issued by the DoPT.
(vi) For regular recruitment, half yearly calendar of recruitment is planned, so that sufficient time is available for
the Institute as well the candidates.
(vii) Recruitment for non-Faculty posts would be carried out by holding combined recruitment for all AIIMS by
clubbing the vacancies for each category of the posts for all AIIMS. The task may be suitably distributed
amongst the AIIMS.
B. Other measures taken earlier by the MoHFW, for increasing the faculty strength in AIIMS are as below :
i. MoHFW has approved for engagement of retired faculty members up to age of70 years on contractual basis
in new AIIMS.
ii. MoHFW has also introduced the scheme of Visiting Faculty/ Guest Faculty to new AIIMS. The new AIIMS
have been empowered to invite visiting faculty from premier institute in India and abroad up to a period of2
years.
iii. The OCI card holders have been allowed to seek appointment on Faculty positions.
iv. New AIIMS have been allowed to take Faculty from Government Medical Colleges/ lnstitutions on
deputation basis.
v. HR sub-committees of the Governing Body(GB)/ Institute Body(IB) have been constituted in all new AIIMS
for speedier approval processes without having to wait for the holding of GB/lB meetings.
C. Policy measures taken to augmetrt resource pool at National level:
In addition, the Ministry has also taken several policy initiatives for bringing about improved availability oftrained HR
at National Level, which are given in U. *l'4b -

D. Non-Faculty posts:
As per the decision taken in the CIB, Recruitment Rules (RR) of AIIMS New Delhi for non-faculty posts are being
followed in new AIIMS to bring uniformity in the RRs across all AIIMS. This would enable combined recruitment for
several AIIMS in one go. Following remedial measures are envisaged to streamline the common recruihrent process
for all non-faculty posts of all AIIMS:
For non-faculty recruitment, the RRs have been made uniform across all AIIMS. This would enable single recruitment
exercise for several AIIMS in one go. The task of carrying out recruitment exercise for different posts has been divided
by distributing posts between 7 AIIMS. Under this arrangement one AIIMS undeftakes recruitment for some posts for
all the new AIIMS. For recruitment ofother non-faculty posts, individual AIIMSwill carry out the recruitment.
E' Following measures are being taken to improve the retention rate of passing out students so that reputation of the
institute as Center of Excellence is reflected:
. Appointment of MBBS graduates of new AIIMS to the post of Junior Resident (lJon Academic) in respective
AIIMS.
o Preference to all MBBS graduates who fulfill Junior Residency (Non Academic) eligibility criteria for JR (Non-
Academics) posts.
o Merit for MBBS graduates can be made on the basis of their aggregate marks in the lst, 2nd and final
professional.
o All Junior Resident (Non Academic) posts which remain vacant after allotment to MBBS graduates of the
Institute can be offered to other candidates, subject to their eligibility.
. Appointment ofCraduates of B.Sc. (Hons.) Nursing courses as Nursing Officer
o Preference to Postgraduate (MD/MS) students ofthe institute for appointment as SR in respective institutes.
E. Following systems and arrangements have been put in place for leveraging the experience of premier medical
institute like AIIMS, JIPMER, PGI, etc. by upcoming AIIMS :
i. New AIIMS are broadly following the guidelines of AIIMS New Delhi. Faculty members of AIIMS New
Delhi, PGIMER Chandigarh, JIPMER Puducherry are regularly sharing their expertise with the faculty
members of new AIIMS.
ii Many ex-Faculty of AIIMS, Delhi PGI, Chandigarh and JIPMER, Puducherry have been appointed as
Members and Presidents of the Institute Body in several new AIIMS with the hope that they will carry the
knowledge of good systems and culture with them and plant these in the new AIIMS.
iii. Expert Faculty of these premier institutes is also associated as experts in the selection committees for
recruitment of Faculff positions.
iv. The 6 new AIIMS are mentoring the other AIIMS now being established and all the support related to
Academics and Recruitment is extended.
v. In the matter of establishing the new AIIMS at Madurai, the officials of JICA which is to support the
establishment of new AllMS, was given exposure of AIIMS Delhi, AIIMS Raipur and AIIMS Jodhpur to
observe the infrastructure, laboratory, academics related works at these institutes to leam lessons from these
institutes.
vi. The Ministry has notified the 'Visiting Faculty Scheme' which can be leveraged by the Institutes to import and
imbibe klowledge, systems and culture.
vii. Other INIs such as PGIME\ JIPMER have been nominated as mentor Institutes for new AIIMS to handhold,
support and guide these new AIIMS in the process of getting established. Mentor Institute will support in early
operationalization of OPD and MBBS batch for the Mentee Institutes. The Mentor Institute will also support
the mentee institutes, in its routine administrative functioning till such time a regular administrative structure is
put in place in the Mentee Institutes.
viii. With a view to redress the issue of Faculty shortage at six new AIIMS, it had been considered that students
with higher qualifications in the field of medicine and passing out of premier institutes could be considered for
appointment on faculty posts at six new AIIMS

1.2 The Committee has been given to understand that earlier the Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare comprised of Department of Health and Department of Family 
Welfare. Both the departments were merged and renamed as Department of Health & 
Family Welfare vide Cabinet Secretariat Notification dated 1 stMarch, 2005 under 
Government of India (Allocation of Business Rules, 1961). It has been pleaded that the  
merger of the two Departments into one was made primarily to facilitate the smooth 
functioning of the Ministry and to avoid duplication of work. The integration of the two 
departments facilitated the integration of the Health and Family Welfare aspects into the 
policy making. The Committee, however, feels that the Department of Health and Family 
Welfare has been entrusted with vast role and responsibilities of implementing a large 
number of Schemes. The Committee, therefore, envisages that there is the need to look into 
the organizational structure of the Department and its scientific and logical organization to 
have focussed and effective implementation of scores of schemes, program me and national 
initiatives. A clue may be taken from the organizational structure of large Ministries like 
the Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Industry. The Committee, in this connection, 
recommends the Ministry to revisit its organizational stru cture and explore the possibility 
of division of its work for effective and result oriented working. The Committee 
recommends that the Government may consider to constitute an Expert Group for detailed 
assessment of the organisation of the Department of He alth and Family Welfare and to 
suggest measures for the purpose.

focussing on the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare but is also looking at the promotive, 
curative and preve ntive aspects of health. As is evident from the Budget document, the 
expenditure part encompasses health and well -being consisting of the Department of Health and 
Family Welfare, Department of Health Research, Ministry of Ayush, Department of Drinking 
water and Sanitation as well as Nutrition because all these factors impinge on human health. In 
addition, it also includes Covid vaccination for which, under Demand No. 40, the Ministry of 
Finance has kept Rs. 35,000 crore for Covid Vaccination and that would eventually flow to the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Therefore, the Department of Health and Family 
Welfare is receiving money from two demands i.e. Rs. 35,000 from Demand No. 40 and Rs.

Challenges being faced by the Department  
2.24 The key challenges faced by the Department include ensuring availability of adequate 
skilled human resources for health, to improve regulatory environment in Medical Education, to 
strengthen health infrastructure, to efficiently monitor public health progr ammes and to ensure 
delivery of quality healthcare services. To address these challenges, the Department has taken 
several initiatives. Some of these are as under:  
 
(i) The National Medical Commission Act was passed by the Parliament in 
August, 2019. The National Medical Commission will steer the reforms in 
medical education. This will include increase in UG & PG seats along with 
improved access to quality and affordable medical education and maintaining 
high ethical standards in medical  profession. 
 
(ii) The Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY) was launched 
to augment the tertiary healthcare capacity in clinical care, medical education and 
research in underserved areas of the country, under which AIIMS like institutions 
are built and  Government Medical Colleges are upgraded by setting -up Super 
Speciality Blocks. 
 
(iii) Primary Healthcare infrastructure is being strengthened through 
implementation of Ayushman Bharat - Health & Wellness Centres and other 
schemes under NHM. 
 

15 
 
(iv) A new Health Manag ement Information System (HMIS) was launched. 
Various IT initiatives have been implemented like NCD App to monitor screening 
of Non -Communicable Diseases, Health and Wellness Centre Portal, and Mera 
Aspatal for tertiary care facilities. 
 
(v) National Quality Assurance Program (NQAP) is being implemented with 
an aim at integrating quality as a dimension in healthcare services with a uniform 
measurement  system. Quality Standards have been laid down for all levels of 
public health  facilities. Performance of each level of facility is envisaged to be 
monitored through Key Performance Indicators. Facilities are incentivized on 
attainment of NQAS  certified status and maintain it. 
2.25 The Committee has been given to understand that the Government has taken sever al 
measures to augment the resources for the health sector and to increase public spending on 
health. These are: 
(i) In 2018-19, Government announced 4% Health & Education Cess in place of 3% 
 Education Cess on personal Income Tax and Corporation Tax, to c ater to the 
 education and health needs of the poor and rural families.  
(ii) In the Union Budget 2020-21, Government announced that the additional 5% cess 
on import of medical devices will be utilized for financing health infrastructure 
and services in aspirational districts. 
(iii) In addition to the budgetary resources, health education and research has access to 
 funding from the Higher Education Funding Agency (HEFA).  
(iv) To tackle the COVID -19 pandemic in India, India COVID -19 Emergency 
Response and Health Systems Preparedness package of Rs. 15000.00 crore was 
approved in April, 2020. The COVID -19 Package, a central sector scheme, is co -
financed by the World Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) and 
Asian Development Bank.  
(v) Further, the Ministry has initiated a new scheme i.e. PM Atma Nirbhar Swasth 
Bharat  Yojna (PM-ASBY) with an outlay of Rs. 64,180 crores over 6 years. This 
is yet to be approved by the Cabinet. The scheme will develop capacities of 
primary, secondary, and tertiary care Health Systems, strengthen existing national 
institutions, and create new institutions, to cater to detection and cure of new and 
emerging diseases.  
(vi) As Public Health is essentially a State subject, States have been advised to 
prioritize allocation to health sector and to increase State sector health spending to 
atleast 8% of  their budget in line with the National Health Policy, 2017.

the sanctioned strength of 585 posts, a total of 147 posts stand vacant. Similarly, against the

Key Concern Areas of SJH and VMMC  
3.28 The Department of Health and Family Welfare apprised the Committee of the Key 
Concern Areas of SJH and VMMC  
(i) Referral policy-There is no efficient referral policy for patients being referred to 
Safdarjung Hospital from nearby primary or tertiary h ealthcare facilities. Valuable hours 
are lost in handling patients with simple diseases which otherwise could be utilized for 
providing specialized care at SJH.   
(ii) Intra-departmental coordination  between NEB & Super Speciality Block is 
hampered by the distance.  A shuttle service for doctors as well as patients is being 
proposed for speedy management.       
(iii) Deficiency of basic facilities -  Against a need of about 40 lac liters a day only 
1/3rd  is being supplied by DJB or NDMC. No permission for tube wells being given by 
DJB.   
 
(iv) Parking - Due to haphazard development of SJH surface parking is woefully short 
causing hardship to the patients/attendants and staff.  Innovative mechanism like stack 
parking has been mooted in the newer blocks.    
(v) Accommodation- A DPR for hostel facilities for resident doctors (782) and 
nurses (1004) has been submitted to Ministry for consideration. A plan for redevelopment 
of staff colony at West Kidwai Nagar & Raj Nagar was proposed by NBCC but could not 
be taken up on nomination basis.   
(vi) Lack of manpower - It has been observed that there is a huge waiting list of 
patient for procedures/operations which can be sorted out by extending the OPD time / 
investigations time and OT time which is only feasible wit h additional manpower.  The 
current manpower is stretched thin and will not be able to sustain the extended hours.  
3.29 The Committee, while taking note of the key concern areas of SJH relating to 
inadequate manpower leading to overstressing of existing h uman resources, inadequate 
hostel facilities, haphazard development of SJH surface parking and lack of referral policy 
leading to loss of valuable hours, recommends provision for adequate manpower, 
immediate approval of DPR hostel facilities for resident d octors (782) and nurses (1004), 
and provision for stack parking in newer blocks etc. to remove some of the stumbling 
blocks for ensuring proper working of the hospital. The Committee also recommends that 
Medical Superintendent of the hospital may be vested with the power to hire staff/faculty 
on contract as per the situational requirement of the Hospital. The Department may also 
consider to extend higher remuneration/incentives with higher qualifications eg DM/MCH 
etc. for ensuring adequate manpower in the hospital.

3.83 The Committee takes note of key strategies suggested to prevent outspread of AIDS and 
STDs in the country:-  
(i) New generation communication strategy focused towards ‘At risk’ and ‘Virtual’ 
 populations with the aim to target at populations not identifying themselves as 
 being at risk and have poor risk perception.  
(ii) Reaching the Missing million - The virtual approach for strengthening the HIV 
 prevention efforts, including access to HIV testing among key and vulnerable 
 populations (High -risk groups and, at -risk adolescents and youth, men and 
 women with high-risk behaviours) seeking partners on virtual platforms. 
(iii) Promoting integrated service delivery through one -stop centres for clinical and 
 behavioural aspects of HIV services as integrated or combination approaches to 
 HIV prevention centralize service provisi on with aim to reduce stigma or 
 logistical barriers.

(iv) Provision of a comprehensive package of services (Sampoorna Suraksha) to 
 reach the last mile plugging the linkage loss at each facility and aiming to 
 provide a comprehensive package of preventive  services to the ‘at -risk’ HIV
