CHAPTER - I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
ADNIMINISTRATIVE MANAGEMENT OF LOCKDOWN & UNLOCKING  
Observation/Recommendation 
1.1 The Committee is of the view that if we had not hit the history books for guidance, the 
reality would have hit us harder. The Government of India learnt from its experience and took 
successful measures like Janta curfew, imposition of 4 months long lockdown and its gradual 
opening, travel restrictions and other social distancing measures to contain the spread of 
Corona virus. The Committee appreciates the measures but also ob serves that there have been 
few glaring lapses in the battle against pandemic like shortage of emergency supplies, red -
tapism, shortage and quality of testing kits, delay in domestic production etc. 
                        (Para 1.42) 
Action Taken 
1.2 Noted. Yes, in the initial phase of the pandemic, there were issues with the indigenous 
capacity in terms of personal protective equipment, N -95 masks, testing kits, ventilators. 
Government of India rose to the occasion and ensured that the local demand fo r the same is met 
through indigenous production as there was global scarcity for all these items.  
1.3 To fast -track informed decision making and to cut down on the procedural delays, 11 
High level Empowered Groups were formed. Based on the evolving needs and scenario in the 
country, on 11th September 2020, these groups were condensed into six larger empowered 
groups (EGs). Four of the EGs are headed by the departmental secretaries and one each by NITI 
Aayog officials. Each EG is tasked with respective func tions: (i) medical infrastructure and 
COVID management plan, (ii) ensuring availability of essential medical equipment and 
augmenting human resources., disease surveillance and testing, (iii) coordinating with the private 
sector, NGOs and international org anizations for response -related activities, (iv) economic and 
welfare measures, (v) information, communication, public awareness, public grievances and data 
management, (vi) strategic issues related to COVID management, and facilitating supply chain 
and lo gistics management. On 8 th January 2021, another Empowered Group on Vaccine 
Administration has been constituted to take all necessary measures for effective implementation 
of CO-WIN platform created for inventory management and delivery of COVID-19 vaccine. 
CONTINGENCY PLAN 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.4 The Committee is of the view that the unprecedented outbreak of Corona  virus required a 
well-planned and coordinated response from the Central as well as State Governments for 
successful containment of the pandemic. There must be an integrated as well as a decentralized 
response to outbreak of pandemic Covid -19 for rescuing t he common masses. The disease trend 
data under IDSP is crucial for generating the required response to contain the outbreak 

3 
 
especially when Inter Sectoral Coordination for zoonotic diseases is one of the main programme 
components of IDSP. The Committee is constrained to observe the failure of National Centre for 
Disease Control -Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (NCDC -IDSP) in generating the 
required response in the wake of the pandemic. The Committee feels that NCDP -IDSP should 
have been utilized in  a more effective manner especially when the sole objective of IDSP is to 
detect and respond to outbreaks in the early rising phase through trained Rapid Response Teams 
(RRTs). The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends for revitalizing the enshrined ro le and 
responsibility of NCDC for effective control of the disease along with strengthening of the 
Central Surveillance Unit (CSU), State Surveillance Units (SSU) and District Surveillance Units 
(DSU). The Committee also recommends the Ministry to effectiv ely implement the various 
programme components under IDSP. The Committee would like the Ministry to launch 
Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme in the remaining States i.e. beyond existing 9 States. 
The Committee observes that there is an urgent need to assess the financial requirement for 
NCDP-IDSP for its revitalization.  
1.5 The Committee, in this connection, strongly recommends the Ministry to chalk out 
strategy and specific course of action to revamp the institutional and Human Resource 
Management structure and further strengthen NCDP -IDSP and pursue with the Ministry of 
Finance for higher budgetary allocation to NCDP-IDSP.  
                                      (Para 2.20) 
Action Taken 
 
1.6 In 2015 Joint Monitoring Mission report of Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme 
(IDSP) recommended review and redesign the IDSP surveillance system, including re -
prioritization of the list of diseases under the IDSP. Subsequently, IDSP, NCDC, re -prioritized 
33 priority health conditions for surveillance. 
1.7 Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) is designed & developed by WHO and 
MoHFW in order to have real time data reported under IDSP and different National Health 
Programmes. It is a web -enabled, near -real-time electronic health information syst em that is 
embedded with all applicable  Government of India's e -Governance standards, Information 
Technology (IT), data &meta data standards to provide state -of-the-art single operating picture 
with geospatial information. 
1.8 IHIP implemented currently in 9 States and has now been expanded to all States in April, 
2021. The IHIP is being aligned with the vision document 2035 and roadmap for public health 
surveillance of NITI Aayog. 
1.9 Under the Atmanirbhar Swasth Bharat, the following interventions at an e stimated outlay 
of Rs. 3060 Crores have been made to strengthen NCDC and public health surveillance & 
response: 
 Strengthening of the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), its 5 regional 
branches and 20 metropolitan health surveillance units 
 Setting up integrated public health labs in all districts and 3382 block public health units 
in 11 States 
 Expansion of the Integrated Health Information Portal to all States/UTs to connect all 
public health labs.  

4 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.10 The Committee believes that contact tracing, testing and isolating are the crucial 
components for Covid -19 containment strategy. The Committee is of the view that poor contact 
tracing and slow testing in the initial phase of pandemic led to the increased number of 
infections in the country. 
                                      (Para 2.26) 
Action Taken 
 
1.11 Noted. During VC‟s, through formal communications and deployment of multi -
disciplinary Central teams, States have been repeatedly advised to increase efforts on contact 
tracing with the target to track, trace and test 30 contacts per confirmed case to stop the chain of 
disease transmission in the country. 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.12 The Committee observes that the Pradhan Mantri Atma Nirbhar Swasth Bharat Yojana is 
an ambitious program of the government that encompasses vital components to consolidate and 
enrich health infrastructure in the country. The Committee recommends that government should 
not leave any stone unturned in implementing its every component to achieve its cherished goal. 
                                     (Para 2.29) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13 Recommendations of the Committee have been noted. 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.14 The Committee observes that the total number of Government hospital beds in the  
country was grossly inadequate keeping in view the rising incidence of Covid-19 cases. Attention 
of the Committee has also been brought to Media Reports which highlighted the abysmally low 
number of beds in Government hospitals in the country especially a t the peak of the pandemic. 
Data from National Health Profile –2019 states that there are total 7,13,986 Government 
hospital beds available in India which amounts to 0.55 beds per 1,000 population. As per 
Reports, 12 States stand below the national level fi gure. The Committee notes that lack of 
hospital beds and the inadequate ventilators further complicated the efficacy of the containment 
plan against the pandemic. As the numbers of cases were on the rise, a frantic search for vacant 
hospital beds became qu ite harrowing. Instances of patients being turned away from 
overburdened hospitals due to lack of vacant beds became the new normal. The scenario of 
patients holding oxygen cylinder rushing from pillar to post in search of bed in AIIMS Patna is a 
testimony to fact that tear apart humanity. The Committee is aggrieved at the poor state of 
healthcare system and therefore, recommends the Government to increase the investment in 
public health and take appropriate steps to decentralize the healthcare services/fac ilities in the 
country.

 ICMR conducted the world‟s largest clinical tria l on benefit of using plasma therapy in

1.30 The Committee is of the view that only those drugs whose efficacy for treating COVID -19 
patients have been established should be used for hospitalized patients and the drugs should be 
prescribed only after multicentric trials and detailed study. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to issue clear guidelines for safe use of drugs. The Committee notes 
that there have been instances where certain drugs were prescribed for COVID -19, but clinical 
trials gave unfavorable results. The  Committee, in this connection, strongly recommends the 
Ministry to issue strict guidelines against use of such drugs when the evidence conclusively 
shows that it does not work for Covid treatment. The Committee believes that only drugs with 
reliable data and research should be used among Covid patients, especially for patients with co -
morbidities.

Management of Post-COVID Complications 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.141 The Committee understands that having defeated the virus is just the beginning of an 
unresearched path of recovery for survivors of severe COVID-19 disease, since COVID 19 is a 
new disease. The post -acute phase of SARS -CoV-2 infection depends on the severity of virus 
attack on different patients. Apart from the fear of unknown, the survivors of COVID 19 venture 
into an unchartered territory o f post COVID complications. Not only do they have to deal with 
fatigue, breathlessness and other physical effects of the disease, but also grapple with the 
psychological impact of it. The Committee is relieved to note that the Government has taken 
cognizance of complexities caused by COVID during post recovery phase and identified 
potential post-acute care needs of recovered COVID -19 patients. The Committee notes that the 
Ministry has adopted integrated holistic approach for managing patients who have recov ered 
from COVID and advised to take care at home. The Committee in this regard recommends the 
Government to put in place healthcare services to ensure a holistic follow -up of post COVID 
treatment of the patients who are showing post COVID complications. It  is also necessary to 
address the possibility of SARS -CoV- 2re-infection, the proportion of adverse reactions after 
hospital discharge and the possible development of other viral and/or bacterial infections. 
                               (Para 6.5)

a need for multidisciplinary care service involving several specialists from both the systems i.e., 
Allopathy and AYUSH system of medi cine for the evaluation and the follow -up of patients 
suffered with COVID-19 disease.

Observation/Recommendation 
1.154 The Committee observes that the limited healthcare infrastructure in the country has 
further been overburdened while coping up with the rising Covid cases in the country. The

should move towards the noble vision of Universal Health coverage. For this to happen, the

Observation/Recommendation 
1.180 The Committee reiterates its  considered view that the healthcare spending in India is 
abysmally low for an emerging economy with a population of 1.3 billion. Lack of desired level of 
investment in the health infrastructure has so far resulted into fragility of Indian health 
ecosystem which posed a big hurdle in generating an effective response against the pandemic. 
The Committee has time and again recommended the Ministry for increasing its spending in the 
health sector for ensuring better health infrastructure and health services to the needy common 
masses. The Committee expresses its serious displeasure over the Government's reluctance to act 
upon the Committee's recommendations in letter and spirit. The Committee is assured that the 
serious impact of the pandemic could have been min imized had the Government over the years 
increased its investment in the healthcare system. The Committee is pained to note the trauma 
and distress the public had to undergo due to absence of a dedicated healthcare system. The 
Committee, therefore, strongl y recommends the Government to increase its investments in the 
public healthcare system and make consistent efforts to achieve the National Health Policy 
targets of expenditure up to 2.5% of GDP within two years as the set timeframe of year 2025 is 
far away and the public health cannot be jeopardized till that time schedule.

believes that a higher budgetary allocation will also boost the healthcare industry and shift the 
focus to Indi an manufacturers and domestic supply chain of products. The Committee believes

2.8 The Committee however differs from the viewpoint of the Ministry as it feels that all the

2.9 The definition of „Mitigation‟, as per Disaster Management Act, 2005, includes measures 
aimed at reducing the risk, impact or effects of a disaster or threatening disaster situation.

whereas a mitigation plan, intends to protect the at-risk population and Vulnerable populations to 
reduce the morbidity and mortality on such populations. Conceptually the two approaches are 
different and hence Ministry of Health & FW continues with its containment plans to 
break/suppress the chain of transmission.

Observation/Recommendation

Further Recommendation 
3.5 In view of the loss of life during the second wave of the Covid -19 pandemic, the 
Committee believes that the measures taken by the Ministry to contain/prevent spread of 
SARS-COV-2 proved to be squarely inadequate. The Committee believes that focus should 
be on strengthening of health infrastructure, ensuring adequate availability of beds, 
adequate supply of oxygen cylinders and essential medicines etc . Besides, the G overnment 
must aggressively keep pushing the vaccination program me in terms of granting approval 
to more vaccines, ramping up vaccines’ production, enhancing delivery capacity and 
increasing the vaccination rate.  
 
3.6 With the incidence of highly mutated Omicron (B.1.1.529) strain of Covid virus, the 
Committee strongly believes that the efficacy of the vaccines must be evaluated. The concerns 
with regards to the new strain developing immunoescape mechanism need to be critically 
addressed. The Committee apprehends that rise in mutations in the virus may lead to reporting 
of more virulent and transmissi ble strain of C ovid virus  in the country . The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to adopt Zero Tolerance C ovid-19 Policy and 
closely track Covid cases across the country.  
 
CONTINGENCY PLAN 
Observation/Recommendation 
3.7 The Committee observes that only 33, 330 and 8,64,517 tests were conducted in the 
month of March and April respectively which increased to 33,878,288 in the month of October. 
The Committee believes that poor contact tracing a nd less testing could have been a factor for 
the exponential growth of COVID cases in the country. The Committee is also worried at the use 

61 
 
of less reliable diagnostic tests which increase the chances of false negatives. Though the Rapid 
Antigen Tests may give faster results but are less reliable than the gold standard RT -PCR tests. 
Large scale use of such tests with low specificity and sensitivity may end up giving false 
negatives and subsequently derail the Covid -19 containment strategy. The Committee is of the 
view that the Government must assess the veracity of Rapid Antigen Test vis -à-vis RT-PCR and 
other diagnostic tests conducted to bring forth the true picture of the testing capacity in the 
country.  
3.8 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to ramp up the testing 
facilities in the country for more accurate tests. The Committee strongly recommends the testing 
rate through the more reliable RT-PCR tests. 
                                    (Para 2.46) 
Action Taken

where the viral load is expected to be high.

recommended.  
o RATs must not take precedence over RT -PCR tests. The use of RATs should be 
restricted to < 30 - 40% in the States.

people is very crucial in reducing the impact of the pandemic  Covid-19. The importance of 
diagnostic testing therefore, cannot be overlooked. An efficient and widely  deployed testing 
mechanism will go a long way in preventing  the spread of the infection . The Committee is 
pained to note that although the second wave came almost six months after the peak of the 
first wave, India’s testing infrastructure remained abysm al and highly insufficient. The 
Committee is of the opinion that to contain pandemic Covid-19 and its mutated strains, 
India must realise its full testing capacity and augment ’s this capacity even further. The 
government should ensure that the testing should  far o utpace the growth of the cases to 
arrest future waves of Covid-19 early.

COVID Management under Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY Scheme 
Observation/Recommendation 
3.66 The Committee notes that NHA has introduced a process of temporary empanelment for 
the hospitals to avail benefits of Ayushman Bharat Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM -JAY) through 
HEM Lite. The Committee welcomes such an initiative considering the gross shortage of 
adequate healthcare facilities. However, the Committee recommends the Ministry to effectively 
scrutinize the whole procedure of temporary empanellement of hospitals so that instances of 
fraudulent healthcare behaviour are avoided. The Committee also recommen ds the Ministry to 
empanel more hospitals especially in areas and States with weak health infrastructure to ensure 
continued supply of essential healthcare services. 
                             (Para 4.14) 
Action Taken 
3.67 The temporary empanelment process using HEM Lite was a special measure in view of 
pandemic-induced circumstances and has ceased to operate now. A total of 535 applications (all 
private) were received under HEM lite module. Out of these, 141 hospitals were empanelled. 
Further, all these hospitals are being moved to draft mode under regular empanelment module. In 
draft mode these hospitals cannot raise fresh pre -authorization request. Standard operating 
procedure will be followed for regularizing their empane lment. For empaneling more hospitals, 
following steps have been taken:   
 All eligible public hospitals including those under the administrative jurisdiction of 
Central Government ministries have been empaneled.   
 A roadmap is being prepared for empaneling majority 100 bed hospitals under the 
scheme. 
 Prominent corporate hospital chains are being approached for empanelment under the 
scheme. In this direction, State Health Agencies have been asked to engage with non -
empaneled hospitals . 

77 
 
 National Health Author ity (NHA) and State  Health Agencies (SHAs) are regularly 
organizing meetings of national and local chapters of Indian Medical Association to seek 
their support in augmenting the role of private healthcare providers . 
  Special incentive over and above the package cost is being provided to NABH accredited 
hospitals.  
3.68 Additionally, a 10% incentive is being given to hospital empaneled in Aspirational 
Districts. This is aimed at attracting investment by private sector in such underserved areas. 
3.69 So far, 24,137 hospitals (including public and private) are empaneled under the scheme. 
Further Recommendation 
3.70 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry  in terms of attracting 
investment by private sector in underserved areas . The Committee desires to know 
whether any assessment has been made with respect  to identifying such areas and S tates 
which need urgent assistance to strengthen their health infrastructure  and incorporating 
the targeted beneficiaries within the ambit of the  Scheme. The Committee seeks to know 
number of hospitals empanelled in the rural areas out of the 141 empanelled hospitals. The 
Committee recommends that more hospitals having facilities to provide emergency services 
arising out of pandemics like Covid -19 should be empanelled in the rural  areas of the 
country.  
Observation/Recommendation 
3.71 The Committee is disappointed to note that many poor people have not been included 
under the scheme due to old SECC data and there is no provision to even update or revise the 
list of beneficiaries. The Committee is not convinced by the argument that State  Governments 
can add beneficiaries at their own cost under State schemes. The Committee believes that States 
generally are fund -starved and it would not be appropriate to lay additional burden on them. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry  and NHA must re -visit the idea of 
revising and updating the list of beneficiaries and not deprive poor strata of society who should 
be given coverage under the scheme. 
                             (Para 4.20) 
Action Taken 
3.72 The beneficiary database under AB-PMJAY has been frozen as per the approval of the 
cabinet and currently there is no mechanism to include additional beneficiaries. The possibility 
of using National Food Security Act (NFSA) data for rationalization and expansion of 
beneficiary base under PMJAY is being explored in consultation with all the stakeholders. Also, 
IT platform, Health Benefit Packages, Empanelled Healthcare providers of PMJAY can also be 
used by other health protection schemes for poor families who may not have figured in  the 
original database. With this in view, National Health Authority (NHA) is actively consulting 
with other Ministries and Departments implementing social security schemes in the country. 
Further Recommendation 

78 
 
3.73 The Committee  fails to comprehend the r ationale behind freez ing the beneficiary 
database and thus depriving the deserving large chunk of poor people from availing the 
benefits of AB -PMJAY, especially in rural areas. The Committee understands that t he 
objective of the scheme can only be fully re alized if the poor people who actually need the 
benefits are enrolled in this scheme at the earliest. The Committee strongly recommends 
the NHA (National Health Authority)  to expand the beneficiary base under the scheme in 
consultation with other Ministries/Departments implementing other social security schemes 
in the country.  
Observation/Recommendation 
3.74 The Committee is of the view that engagement of both private and public sector is a must 
for ensuring robust delivery of healthcare services under the  Scheme ABPMJAY. The Committee 
understands that Covid treatment rate and charges for other health package for small private 
hospitals may not be sustainable which would discourage private hospitals from empanelling 
under the Scheme. The Committee therefore  recommended the Ministry to rationalize the 
package rates especially in rural areas where people suffer due to a weak primary healthcare 
infrastructure. 
                             (Para 4.29) 
Action Taken 
3.75 Revision of benefit packages listed under AB-PMJAY is a continuous process based on 
feedback received from respective stakeholders. NHA has a dedicated medical cell which is 
consulted for technical inputs. The inputs of the medical cell are then put up to the respective 
review committee. Post that  States are consulted for understanding their views. Finally, the 
inputs are provided to the NHA Governing Board for making a decision. Further, State

testing and treatment based on guidelines issued by NHA.

engaging both private and public sector for ensuring robust delivery of healthcare services 
under the Scheme Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY).

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS - AT A GLANCE 
 
ADMINISTRATIVE MANAGEMENT OF LOCKDOWN & UNLOCKING 
 In view of the loss of life during the second wave of the Covid -19 pandemic, the 
Committee believes that the measures taken by the Ministry to contain/prevent spread of 
SARS-COV-2 proved to be squarely inadequate. The Committee believes that focus should 
be on strengthening of health infrastructure, ensuring adequate availability of beds, 
adequate supply of oxygen cylinders and essential medicines etc. Besides, the Government 
must aggressively keep pushing the vaccination programme in terms of granting appr oval 
to more vaccines, ramping up vaccines’ production, enhancing delivery capacity and 
increasing the vaccination rate.  
(Para 3.5) 
 With the incidence of highly mutated Omicron (B.1.1.529) strain of Covid virus, the 
Committee strongly believes that the efficacy of the vaccines must be evaluated. The 
concerns with regards to the new strain developing immunoescape mechanism need to be 
critically addressed. The Committee apprehends that rise in mutations in the virus may 
lead to reporting of more virulent and transmissible strain of Covid virus in the country. 
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to adopt Zero Toleran ce 
Covid-19 Policy and closely track Covid cases across the country.  
(Para 3.6) 
CONTINGENCY PLAN 
The Committee believes that timely detection and isolation of potentially infectious 
people is very crucial in reducing the impact of the pandemic Covid -19. The importance of 
diagnostic testing therefore, cannot be overlooked. An efficient and widely deployed testing 
mechanism will go a long way in preventing the spread of the infection. The Committee is 
pained to note that although the second wave came almost six months after the peak of the 
first wave, India’s testing infrastructure remained abysmal and highly insufficient. The 
Committee is of the opinion that to combat current pandemic Covid -19 and other future 
emergencies, India must realise its full testing  capacity and augment’s this capacity even 
further. The government should ensure that the testing should far outpace the growth of 
the cases to arrest future waves of Covid-19 early.  
 (Para 3.11) 
 The Committee also notes that with the new strain of Covid, Omicron (B.1.1.529) 
exhibiting 30+ mutations, tracking and testing facilities especially at airports must also be 
strengthened and rigorous testing and screening of travelers must be carried out. The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry to explore imposing travel restrictions and 
isolating passengers from 'at -risk' countries, as part of their new covid strain containment 
strategy. With WHO designating Omicorn as "Variant of Concern", the Governme nt must 
take immediate measures to prevent the transmission of any newer strains in the country.  
(Para 3.12) 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation for creation of the 'Indian Health 
Service' (IHS) in the Center and across States as a dedicated, effi cient, and adequately 

94 
 
resourced public health cadre on the pattern of Indian Administrative Service (IAS). It also 
recommends that the Ministry should issue specific guidelines to the states regarding timely 
payment of wages to the healthcare workers parti cularly who are the foot soldiers of the 
healthcare system. The Committee further strongly advocates for strengthening the 
network of ASHAs, ANMs and other community health workers and the necessary support 
in the healthcare delivery system. The Committee underlines the need to expedite the 
reforms in regulatory mechanism of dental and nursing education.  
(Para 3.20) 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that the recent Second Wave of the Covid -
19 saw unprecedented price escalation and shortage of oxygen  cylinder and other critical 
equipments and drugs. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Governments must 
set up adequate Oxygen manufacturing plants and a robust supply and support mechanism 
for States to ensure uninterrupted supply of oxygen and other medical equipments and 
drugs for use under emergency situation. The Committee is also concerned about the 
exorbitant prices of the critical medicines during pandemics. Given the fact that the 
National Pharmaceutical Pricing  Authority (NPPA) updates t he price caps of such 
medicines and drugs, the Committee, recommends a strict and regular monitoring over 
adherence to this price capping, especially in the event of pandemic like situation.  
(Para 3.26)

importance of bio-medical waste collection, management and its disposal. Now -a-days, the 
management of biomedical waste has become a major concern as bio -medical waste is 
being generated not only from hospitals but also from househol ds. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends, that the capacity of the 200 odd Common Bio -medical Waste 
Treatment Facilities (CBWTF) spread across the nation must be augmented for their 
optimal utilisation. The ULBs (Urban Local Bodies), concerned authorities and other 
stakeholders must be directed to ensure minimal leakages in the waste (bio -medical) 
journey from point of origin to disposal. States need to be sensitized about the guidelines of 
disposal of biomedical waste. For this to happen, proper training a nd awareness 
programmes should be organized at the district and block level to educate both the workers 
of municipalities and the public at large for better bio-medical waste management.  
(Para 3.31)

and assessment pertaining to key performance indicators related to surveillance, testing, 
hospital infrastructure, logistics at the district levels. The Committee obs erves that the 
steps taken to combat the second wave of pandemic were not sufficient and more concrete 
action could have been undertaken to contain the impact of Covid -19. The Committee 
believes that structural and operational corrections are required to p repare for the future 
health emergencies. The Committee, therefore, recommends that every State should 
establish at least one medical college and hospital as 'Centre of Excellence' for proper 
health surveillance during emergency situation.

I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One Hundred Thirty -First Report of the Committee on Action Ta ken by 
Government on the Recommendations/ Observations contained in One Hundred Twenty Eighth 
Report on Demands for Grants 2021-22 (Demand No. 4) of the Ministry of AYUSH.  
2. The One Hundred Twenty Eighth Report of the Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on 
the Table of Lok Sabha on 17 th March, 2021.  Action Taken Notes of the Government on the 
recommendations contained in the Report was received from the Ministry on 16th June, 2021.   
3.  The Committee made a total of 53 recommendations in its 128 th Report. Out of the 53 
recommendations, a total number of 21 recommendations have been accepted by the Ministry, 
has been categorized under Chapter I and there are a total number of 10 recommendations, which 
the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Ministry‘s replies, has been categorized 
under Chapter II. A total number of 19 recommendations/ observations in respect of which 
replies of the Ministry have not been acce pted by the Committee and the Committee has made 
further recommendations thereon, has been categorized under Chapter III while a total number of 
3 recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been 
received, has been categorized under Chapter IV. 
4. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 
the 1st  December, 2021.

II.    MACRO ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATION  
Recommendation 
1.8 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the sharp shortfall in allocation of the 
Ministry as compared to the projected demand, despite its repeated recommendation for 
increasing the budgetary allocation of the Ministry, keeping in view the scope, reach and value 
AYUSH can add to the health of the people. Given its indigenous/traditional element, cost 
effectiveness and a safe alternative to modern system of medicine, the Ministry of AY USH, 
through its schemes and strategies, can help AYUSH system of healthcare to emerge as a 
valuable system of medicine in healthcare delivery. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that 
budgetary constraints should not be allowed to act as a stumbling block to achieve the mission 
objectives to position AYUSH system as the primary and preferred system of healthcare in India. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate budgetary support be provided to the 
Ministry as and when required by it. 
(Para 2.3)

Secretary (AYUSH)‘s D.O. letter No.H -11013/9/2021-Budget dated29.04.2021  for providing 
adequate budgetary support to this Ministry.

1.16 The Committee observes that the allocation for Ministry of AYUSH is 4.17% of the 
Health Budget as against 3.26% of the Health Budget in 2020-21 and the increase witnessed this 
year is negligible. The Committee has been recommending, time and again, that at least 5% of 
the total Health Budget should be earmarked for Ministry of AYUSH. Thou gh the percentage of 
allocation to the Ministry of AYUSH in comparison to Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
has marginally improved and crossed 4 percent mark but this is not adequate. To establish 
Ayush as an effective alternative system of medicine, budgetary resources will have to be 
comparatively increased to provide a level playing field. The Committee believes that AYUSH 
systems of medicine are the treasure of country’s traditional knowledge systems which need to be 
re-discovered and promoted. At a time, when the whole world is dealing with pandemic Covid -
19, the vital role of Indian Systems of Medicine owing to their effective prophylactic usage 
cannot be underestimated. Needless to say, the AYUSH Systems are integrative and economical 
systems of medicine which need financial support so as to tap its full potential and proliferation 
at Panchayatlevel. The Committee, accordingly, reiterates its earlier recommendation of 
increasing budget of AYUSH Ministry to at least 5% of the budget of Health Minis try at the RE

allocate 10% of the Health Budget to Ministry of AYUSH from the next financial year

1.32 The Committee is deeply disappointed with the status of manpower in the 36 SMPBs. 
Apart from Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan, there is no separate regular post sanctioned 
by respective State Government for SMPBs. The shortage of manpower in SMPBs is a matter of 
serious concern as the NMPB, being the nodal agency for medicinal plants cannot function 
alone without the active supp ort of SMPBs. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the 
Ministry that issue of shortage of manpower in SMPBs should be taken up with the States/UTs 
and they may be convinced of the importance of having separate manpower for SMPBs. The 
Ministry should also  have guidelines wherein minimum number of manpower required in a 
SMPB be laid down clearly so that the SMPB understand the need to give the support to the 
NMPB as well as involve itself fully in the promotion of the medicinal plants of that State. The 
Committee strongly believes that the schemes of medicinal plant can not be implemented 
properly till a robust structure in the States (SMPBs) with adequate funds and full time 
manpower is made available. The Committee, therefore, exhorts the Ministry to persu ade the 
States/UTs to have separate full time manpower for SMPBs for better operational efficacy.

1.77 The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry must ensure stringent implementation 
of Pharmacovigilance schemes. For th is, the Committee recommends that the education -related 
to Pharmacovigilance should be included in the curriculum itself and periodic awareness 
programmes should be organized for both health care professionals and patients. Moreover, 
monthly reporting of A DRs (Adverse Drug Reactions) reports should be made mandatory at all

updated medicine literature database would provide credible and latest medical information to

reiterate that all these measures can only be realized if the Pharmacovigilance network is

3.1 The Committee takes note of the efforts made by Ministry in achieving its objective of 
“Health for all” during 2020 -21 under NAM and Information, Education and Communication 
Schemes by way of providing cost  effective AYUSH services and also to strengthen and 
popularize AYUSH systems at the grass root level. The Committee, however, feels much more 
needs to be done towards making AYUSH healthcare facilities accessible to all and making its 
presence felt in rur al and remote areas of the country. There have however, been doubts and 
questions regarding the efficacy of Indian systems of medicine. Even though the popularity and 
presence of AYUSH systems is increasing, the need of the hour is to lay focus on standard ization 
of academic courses and scientific validation of AYUSH system. The Committee desires the 
Ministry to focus on standardization of quality of AYUSH healthcare services, quality control of 
AYUSH drugs, strengthening of drug testing laboratories, pharm acies and improving the quality 
of AYUSH education in the country so as to position AYUSH as a true alternative system of 
medicine.

IV. MAINSTREAMING OF AYUSH SYSTEM 
Recommendation 
3.91 The Committee acknowledges the initiatives taken by the Ministry of AYUSH through its 
various institutes in mainstreaming AYUSH systems of medicine. However, the Committee is of 
the opinion that the maj ority of the work done is preventive in nature and recommends that the 
Ministry should encourage and create a detailed roadmap for establishing AYUSH systems of 
medicine as a curative alternative to the Allopathic system. The Committee believes that the 
Ministry should do more than organizing seminars, conferences, meetings, workshops, road 
shows etc. to bring some tangible progress in the adoption of Indian traditional systems. The 
Committee notes the main reason behind the poor export of Indian traditiona l drugs is their 
failure to meet global norms on safety and efficacy. The Committee also notes that licensing of 
Ayurvedic drugs is a State subject, so there is a lack of uniformity in the approach of different 
States.

a snail's pace.  The Committee, in this connection, strongly recommends that the creation 
of vertical structure for AYUSH under CDS CO should be expedited and the recruitment 
process be completed at the earliest.   
(Para 3.47)  
  The Committee notes that W.H.O Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) has been 
given to 21 Ayurvedic  Drug manufacturers to export their products as per standards and 
other requirements of importing countries. The Committee expects the Ministry to monitor 
whether these 21 manufacturers have in house quality control section and drug testing 
laboratory as p er the schedule 'T' of prescribed Good Manufacturing Practices. The 
Committee would like to be apprised whether any complaints with respect to sub -standard 
or inferior products has/have been received against existing licensed manufacturers in the 
last two years and the action taken against the manufacturers violating the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Rules, 1945. The Committee, at the same time, recommends the Ministry to 
effectively operationalise the E -Aushadhi portal by activating new application process for 
online registration and license application in order to achieve the set objectives of the 
portal.  
(Para 3.51)  
  The Committee observes that during 2021 -22, an amount to the tune of Rs. 4.10 
crore has been allotted to further strengthen the Pharmacovigilance network and reporting 
mechanism by establishing more peripheral Pharmacovigilance centers i.e. upto 100 by 
ensuring adequate manpower for Pharmacovigilance Centres across the country. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to make an assessment of the operat ional cost of each 
Pharmacovigilance Centre along with the number of workforce required to run it smoothly 
and accordingly project its fund requirement for the scheme.  The Committee recommends 
the Ministry to comply with the findings and observations of t he Comprehensive Impact 
Assessment of the Pharmacovigilance Scheme for its effective execution and actual 
achievement of set objectives on the ground level.  
(Para 3.54)  
 The Committee notes that the various Councils of AYUSH and their institutes are in 
the process of obtaining their NABH accreditation.  The Committee, however, reiterates 
that a timeframe for completing NABH accreditation must be fixed by the Ministry and 
desired the Ministry to keep a close watch to ensure the compliance of NABH standards  by 
those who have been accredited. 
(Para 3.79)  

76 
 
  The Committee is well aware of the grant -in-aid that is given under National 
AYUSH Mission under the component of Quality Control of ASU&H Drugs to State 
ASU&H licensing Authorities/Drug Controllers for technical manpower. The Committee 
wonders that the Ministry is silent on the recommendation of the Committee relating to 
creation of a specialized body for AYUSH Drug Control with requisite expertise at the 
State level on lines of the vertical structure for AYUSH under CDSCO. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Ministry to reconsider its recommendation and also explore the 
feasibility of setting up of a specialized body especially for AYUSH Drugs Control at the 
State Level.  
(Para 3.82)  
  The Committee expresses its pleasure that various research institutes are 
undertaking clinical trials for making their research scientific and evidence based.  Such 
clinical trials help to reach a firm conclusion that a par ticular drug is both safe and 
effective.  The Committee is of the considered view that the Indian system of Medicine 
would get a big boost if quality and evidence based scientific research is carried out.  The 
Committee, in this connection, recommends the Ministry to develop a robust Clinical Trial 
Management System (CTMS) in AYUSH systems that would enable researchers to seek 
better ways to utilize each other research outcomes and thus create a platform for sharing 
the database and the experience gained with each other for better R&D outcome.  
(Para 3.90)  
MAINSTREAMING OF AYUSH SYSTEM 
  The Committee takes into account the significant R&D and public health initiatives 
undertaken by various Councils of AYUSH to harness the potential of AYUSH systems.  
The C ommittee appreciates that collaborative research studies with different countries 
would help in establishing the system as the credible and scientific system of medicine 
which may emerge as a curative alternative to modern medicines.  The Committee, 
however, is disappointed to note that the Ministry has not given any information about 
reasons for poor export of ASU&H drugs. The Committee's concerns about ASU drugs 
failing to meet global norms on safety and efficacy have not been addressed.  The 
Committee is  also surprised that the Ministry has not paid attention to the point 
highlighted by it regarding lack of uniformity in the approach of different States with 
respect to ASU Drugs as Health is a State subject.  The Committee emphasises that given 
the increa sing popularity of AYUSH systems especially during pandemic Covid -19, it is 
high time to showcase the effectiveness of ASU&H drugs in domestic market as well as 
global arena. The Committee recommends the Ministry to have a standard licensing 
process based on uniform parameters across all the States so that the drug formulations do 
not vary in different States and also conform to global norms of safety and efficacy. This 
would go a long way in establishing Indian System of Medicine as an alternative system o f 
medicine.  
(Para 3.119)  
  The Committee is constrained to note that the Ministry has not paid attention to the 
area of concern regarding lack of prompt action in response to misleading and unfounded 
advertisements about AYUSH drugs/products. The Committ ee had recommended for 

77 
 
making the provisions of both Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Magical Remedies Act stricter 
so as to dissuade drugs manufacturers from giving misleading advertisement about 
AYUSH products.  The Committee, in this connection, reiterates t hat the licensing 
authorities and State Drug Controllers should have adequate powers to take prompt and 
stern action against such misconduct under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Magical 
Remedies Act. The Committee further recommends the Ministry to come u p with 
appropriate amendments in the concerned legislations accordingly.  
(Para 3.122)  
 The Committee appreciates the various initiatives of the Ministry of AYUSH to 
promote and develop Indian system of Medicine.  Given the vast potential of Indian System 
of Medicine in contemporary times and especially during pandemic Covid -19, the 
Committee believes that Indian System of Medicine has huge capacity to position itself as 
an effective and economical system of medicine as an alternative to modern system of 
medicine. This will help reduce out of pocket expenditure on health.  The Committee 
recommends the Ministry to identify the 'Key Concern Areas' especially with regard to 
quality of education and research, drugs and overall healthcare delivery systems in 
AYUSH institutions. The Committee recognizes the importance of collaborative researches 
as well as clinical trials for better research outcomes. Since Ayurveda is the valued heritage 
of the glorious past of our country, it needs proper propagation at the grass-root and global 
level. The Committee, in this regard, recommends the Ministry to lay sp ecial focus on the 
regulation and control over safety and efficacy of Ayurveda drugs and products to enable 
the market of the AYUSH products grow internationally and stand to any scientific 
scrutiny.  Keeping in view the vast arena of AYUSH systems, the Co mmittee recommends 
the Ministry to chalk out specific course of action to combat the challenges ahead for 
strengthening the infrastructure, education and practice of AYUSH systems and expand 
the reach of these systems across the country and abroad.  
(Para 3.126)

PREFACE 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One Hundred Thirty -Second Report of the Committee on Action Taken by 
the Government on the Recommendations/ Observations contained in the 127 th Report on on 
Demands for Grants 2021 -22 (Demand No. 45) of the Department of Health Research (DHR), 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.  
2. The One Hundred Twenty Seventh Report of the Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on 
the Table of Lok Sabha on 8 th March, 2021.  The Action Taken Notes of the Government on t he 
recommendations contained in the Report was received from the Departments on 10 th August, 
2021.   
3.  The Committee made a total of 51 recommendations in the 127 th Report, out of which  23 
recommendations have been accepted by the Ministry and has been categorized under Chapter I. 
There are 10 recommendations, which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the 
Ministry‟s replies that have been categorized under Chapter II. There are 14 recommendations/ 
observations, in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been accepted by the 
Committee and the Committee has made further recommendations thereon and has been 
categorized under Chapter III while 4 recommendations/observations in respect of which final 
replies of the Ministry have not been received, has been categorized under Chapter IV. 
4. The Committee, in its meeting held on the  1st December, 2021 considered the Draft 
Report and adopted the same.

CHAPTER–I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
Recommendation 
1.1 The Committee observes that the Covid -19 pandemic has created the need for 
transformation of the allocation of budgetary resources for research and innovation in the health 
sector. The Department of Health Research being the nodal department for medical re search 
needs to reorient its focus in strengthening research capabilities and infrastructure and 
reinvigorating interest in medical research amongst the youth. Availability of up -to-date, 
sophisticated, state of the art research infrastructure will provide  impetus to research and 
innovation. These insights help in formulating group or population -specific policies. 
Technologically backed, swift and accurate testing & diagnostic services will effectively counter 
existing and emerging viral diseases. Incorpora ting niche technologies like ML and AI in 
understanding human behaviour and tendencies can generate qualitative insights into issues like 
how human behaviour impacts the transmission of diseases. The Covid -19 pandemic has made 
us realize that there is an u rgent need for improving infrastructure for enhancing bio -security in 
the country by strengthening testing and research facilities. The Department of Health Research 
needs to ramp up its resources and strategic research priorities. 
(Para 1.6) 
Action Taken 
1.2 Important initiatives taken by the Department of Health Research (DHR) and ICMR for 
improving infrastructure, strengthening bio -security as well as improving innovations are as 
follows: 
 Creating National Network for Clinical Trials utilizing the services of Multi -Disciplinary 
Research Units (MRUs) in Government Medical Colleges and Model Rural Health 
Research Units (MRHRUs).   
 Establishment of 30 MRUs and 11 MRHRUs during the 15th Finance  Commission 
period (2021 -22 to 2025 -26) in addition to 85 MRUs and 28 MRHRUs already 
established upto 31.03.2021. 
 Establishment of 42 more Viral Research & Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) during the 
15th Finance Commission period (2021 -22 to 2025 -26) in ad dition to 124 VRDLs 
already established upto 31.03.2021.  
 Establishment of 15 new „DHR -ICMR Advanced Molecular Oncology Diagnostic 
Services‟ (DiaMonds) Centres in addition to 9 existing Centers under the scheme of 
Human Resource & Capacity Development Scheme.  
 About 2800 Laboratories in medical colleges/ institutes/ private sector for COVID testing 
have been made functional. 
 Need- based custom platforms developed for COVID -19 testing (RT -PCR, True NAT, 
CBNAAT, Antigen testing, mobile vans, home testing). 
 Developed COVID KAWACH Elisa, first indigenous human IgG ELISA kit for SARS -
CoV-2 antibodies diagnosis. 
 Developed fully indigenous COVID -19 vaccine, Covaxin in collaboration with Bharat 
Biotech. Has been rolled out.

 With a view to ramp up and prioritize the research activities, following additional 
initiatives are proposed: 
 Establishment of Regional Research Platform for South East Asian Region Countries for 
collaboration in health research in partnership with WHO and 10 countries of SE Asia to 
combat emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases in SE Asia Region. 
 Establishment of Centre for One Health at Nagpur. 
 Setting up of 4 Zonal Institutes of Virology for North -East, North, South and Central 
Zones.  
 Setting up of National Centre for Assistive Health Technology at AIIMs/IITs.  
1.3 Setting up of ICMR -Centres of Excellence at the IITs for boosting innovation and 
product development in the domain of medical devices and diagnostics.

to allocate 5percent of the budget of the Department of Health & Family Welfare to DHR at the 
R.E. stage. 
  
       (Para 2.5)

III. ICMR 
Recommendation 
1.6 The Committee appreciates the ICMR’s track record with respect to the utilization of 
funds. Barring the year 2020 -21, the ICMR has a near -perfect track -record of utilizing the 
budgeted funds. The Committee, however, is surprised to note that the grant that ICMR receives 
is less than the actual allocation that the DHR get s in the name of ICMR. It is quite intriguing to 
the Committee that while on the one hand the Ministry of Finance does not allocate the fund as 
per the projected demand and even the allocated fund is not released in totality to the ICMR. The 
Committee opines that the role of ICMR is very crucial considering the current and future health 
challenges; inadequacy of funds to ICMR can undermine the desired outcomes in the health 
sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient funds must be released to ICMR 
including additional funds, at the RE stage. 
(Para 3.4)

1.33 Following actions have been taken by the ICMR to promote studies in this regard: 
i. Prevalence of fluorosis in the community of selected districts of India and development 
of an appropriate intervention model for prevention and control of fluorosis‟ was a Task 
Force Study under the Centre for Promotion of Nutrition Research and Training (CNRT) 
– ICMR HQ. ICMR-NIN, Hyderabad conducted the study in Prakasam district of Andhra 
Pradesh. Dental fluorosis screening was done in 60,000 population from 30 villages and 
the data was shared with ICMR for analysis 
ii. Similarly, Vitamin -A Deficiencies data was collected as part of the ICMR Task Force

for the longitudinal study and coordinated and implemented the same in Telangana State. 
The data collection (demographic, health, WASH, releva nt pregnancy, child birth and 
lactation related data, diet and anthropometry) and sample collection (blood, urine and 
household salt samples for relevant biomarker estimations) from 200 pregnant women 
recruited from 100 villages from the district of Yadadr i/Bhuvanagiri has been completed 
(including data scrutiny) during all the six study time points (2017 to 2020). The data and 
samples have been shared with the Centre for Promotion of Nutrition Research and 
Training – (CNRT), ICMR, New Delhi and analysis is in progress. 
1.34 ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition agrees with the recommendation of the committee 
and would take up such studies in future on a continuous basis in regular time intervals so as to

calamities for efficient management and control of the health emergencies . and effective control

Recommendation 
1.42 The Committee recommends that to enhance its performance in disease surveillance and 
monitoring the Department must focus on the following priority areas: - 
 Network of laboratories should be equipped with the latest tool and technology and 
increase of testing capabilities; 
 Expeditious detection of viruses so as to initiate timely and effective health interventions; 
 Training in handling high risk pathogens; 
 Testing labs in under-served and difficult terrains; 
 Strengthening of laboratory quality systems through quality control quality assurance; 
 Capacity building of health care facilities etc. 
(Para 4.12) 
Action Taken 
1.43     The network has 124 Virus Research and Diagnosis laboratories (10 Regional, 25 State 
Level, 89 Medical College level) established across the country. The laboratories have state -of-
art infrastructure and are equipped with modern machinery required for  virus research and 
diagnosis. All the VRDLs have notable testing capacities for all viruses of public health 
importance. 
 All VRDLs have trained manpower and equipped with requisite infrastructure needed for 
detection of early diagnosis of viruses. The VRD Ls are now capable to diagnose the 
viruses within 12-48 hour depending on the complexity of the tests. 
 Trainings on handling High Risk pathogen and Biosafety & Biosecurity are routinely 
being conducted at National Institute of Virology, Pune and other equi pped Regional & 
State level VRDLs 
 Geographical coverage for virus diagnosis has already been taken care while site 
selection. Furthermore, efforts will be taken care to cover difficult terrains if some left 
untouched. 

11 
 
 Various QA/QC, EQA programmes for diff erent viruses are already under 
implementation. 
 VRDL resource center (NIV -Pune and NIE Chennai) as well as the Regional VRDLs 
organizes training programs for capacity building in lab diagnosis, outbreak investigation, 
reporting etc.  
Recommendation 
1.44 The Committee is of the view that a full proof surveillance system of DHR can help in 
timely identification of viruses and timely health intervention for the same. Further, the 
Committee believes that the DHR along with Department of Health and Family welfar e should 
formulate a concrete contingent plan to control infections before turning into pandemics/ 
epidemics. The level of preparedness must be resilient enough to contain the outbreak of 
epidemics and calamities so that precious human lives could be saved. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends establishing a robust and highly advance surveillance system for high -risk 
pathogens for early detection, response and research on an immediate call. In addition to this, 
the DHR should also create a trained workforce  for handling infectious disease pathogens of 
public health importance. 
1.45 To further strengthen the contingent plan for managing epidemic and National 
calamities, VRDLs must be trained in Good Clinical Laboratory Practices (GCLP). 
(Para 4.15) 
Action Taken 
1.46 Now 124 VRDLs have been set up against the target of 125.  Hence the target set for the 
14th Finance Commission period has almost been achieved. 
1.47 The scheme has been further continued for the 15th Finance Commission period (2021 -
22 to 2025 -26) with the target to establish another 42 VRDLs (1 Regional, 2 State Level, 39 
Medical College), bringing the total number to 166 VRDLs upto 2021 -26. This will expand the 
coverage to the entire country and will definitely help in future Epidemic and National 
Calamities and for fast tracking of viral outbreaks/surveillance.  
1.48 Good Clinical Laboratory Practices (GCLP) training is a regular component for this 
activity. More trainings in GCLP will be conducted in future. 
 
Recommendation 
1.49 Keeping in view the pandemic Covid -19 and the response time of the concerned  
Departments/agencies, the Committee underlines the need for establishment of more 
sophisticated labs in different parts of the country. The Committee has been given to  understand

established. The Committee recommended that in order to cater to the  testing needs of the 
different zones of the country, at least one lab of BSL -IV category in  each zone should be 
established. 
(Para 4.16)

IV. Schemes/ Projects of Department of Health Research (DHR) 
Recommendation 
1.51 The Committee takes serious note of the fact that not a single MRU has been established 
this financial year. The Committee also notes with concern that out of the total approved 80 
MRUs for establishment, research work has commenced only in 47 MRUs. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that DHR should speed u p the processes to attain the target of 
establishing 10 MRUs in the current financial year. The Committee also recommends that the 
Government should expedite approvals for MRUs that are at various stages of consideration. In 
addition to this, the Committee also recommends that research work in remaining 33 established 
MRUs must commence at the earliest. 
(Para 4.21) 
Action Taken 
1.52 Five new MRUs were established before the close of the year 2020 -21, taking the total

MRUs were diverted to managing the COVID -19 pandemic related functions.  The matter is, 
however, being pursued with the MRUs to increase the pace of research related functions and it 
is expected that the research work would soon commence in all the remaining MRUs. 
1.53 The target for financial year 2021 -22 is to set up 6 MRUs and constant efforts are being 
made to achieve that target. 
 
Recommendation

scheme/activities to analyze evidence related cost -effectiveness and clinical effectiveness for the 
deployment of health technologies covering medicines, devices and health programmes, are 
undertaken, which in turn ensures effective and optimal utilization of health budget and easy 
access to quality healthcare at the minimum cost. Its main objective is to reduce out of pocket 
expenditure and address inequality. The Committee, therefore, recommends optimal utilization 
of allocated funds to  minimize the cost for quality healthcare, especially in rural, urban slums 
and tribal areas. 
(Para 4.42) 
 
 

13 
 
Action Taken 
1.55 An allocation of Rs.15.00 crores was made in RE 2020 -21 for Health Technology 
Assessment in India (HTAIn ) and the utilization was Rs.13.66 crores (about 93.4%).  Budget 
allocated for HTAIn for the year 2021-22 is about Rs. 23 crores. 
1.56 Studies have been undertaken under HTAIn for optimal utilization of allocated funds to 
minimize the cost for quality healthcare, in rural as well as urban areas, as follows:   
1. Safety Engineered syringes for therapeutic care in India has supported the allocation of 
funds to interventions that will help save budget by preventing needle prick blood borne 
infection like Hepatitis and HIV 
2. Early Screening for cervical cancer study will help in early diagnosis of the disease and 
reduce mortality 
3. Neonatal Screening for identifying hearing impairment in infants will help in precise

4. Other studies have been undertaken to identify safer long -term contraceptives for family

Recommendation 
1.57 The Committee understands that due to problems posed by Covid -19, the funds could not 
be utilised fully. The Committee, however, is of the view that despite certain restriction due to the

Recommendation 
3.1 The Committee is of the opinion that a crucial body like DHR cannot be made to suffer 
due to shortage of administrative staff when the country is confronting the annual  epidemic of 
Dengue, Chikungunya, Japanese Encephalitis etc. added by the outbreak of  new viruses. 
Optimum utilization of the allocated budget and actual efficiency of the Department can only be 
realized when it functions at its full capacity.  The work and  responsibility of the Department 
have increased tremendously due to Covid-19 and a significant number of other strains reported 
worldwide. The Committee agrees with the  Department that to deal with future pandemic 
situations there is a need to bring more  professionalism in the Department and such objectives 
can be achieved by having more  scientific staff; enhanced capacity of experts through skill 
integration, provision of  incentives through rewards, etc. 
(Para 1.10) 
Action Taken

Scientists „C‟, „D‟ and „E‟ (2 posts each) for the Deptt. of  Health Research.  Recruitment Rules

will bring more professionalism in the Department.

practices and formulate a mechanism for completing the recruitment process within a 
definite time frame.

forcefully take up the matter with the Department of Health & Family Welfare, Department of 
Personnel & Training and Department of Expenditure to fill up the vacant  posts and also to

Department to accede to the genuine requests of the Department inthis regard in a time -bound 
manner. The Committee also believes that the Department  needs to work in close coordination 
with the Department of Health & Family Welfare (DoH&FW),  Department of Biotechn ology 
(DBT), CSIR-Centre for Cellular & Molecular Biology(CCMB)  and other similar organizations 
involved in health research  so as to establish a sync between Research -Policy-Public Health

research and investigation.

3.57 The Committee endorses the Expert Committee’s view that the latest data for India was  
not used in computing various indicators of GHI and also appreciates the Expert Committee for 
trying to remove the lacunae in measuring hunger by involving other concerned Ministries. The 
Committee believes that there should be objective assessment and proper measuring of hunger to 
generate the actual and real data on hunger. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
research concerning a specific Hunger Index that is more suitable to India’s dynamics and 
demography must be undertaken. 
(Para 3.43) 
Action Taken 
3.58 None of the indicators used in Global Hunger Index (GHI) specifically measures 
„Hunger‟. The methodology is flawed and data used are of sub -optimal accuracy. The Index 
intended to assess the status for entire population is giving excessive weightage to under -five 
children. There is a need to develop a robust and acceptable country specific methodology to 
measure hunger on priority and avoid using proxy indicators for hunger.  
3.59 In order to do so, the data on the actual diets and consumpti on of foods along with the 
indicators like population undernutrition, and child mortality etc need to be available from time 
to time. While CNNS data is the latest on children‟s nutrition status, there is hardly any data on 
national level prevalence of pop ulation undernutrition and dietary intakes. The most recent data 
available is from NNMB-NIN reported in the year 2012 for rural population (10 states) and 2016 
for urban population (16 districts).  
3.60 Such large-scale data collection should be taken up o n continuous basis for developing 
robust methodologies and datasets for ascertaining hunger status and development of country -
specific hunger index. ICMR -NIN can certainly take lead in doing it on a project basis from 
time-to-time. 

33

3.61 The Committee is in agreement with ICMR regarding  the need for  adopting a 
robust, acceptable country specific methodology to measure hunger on priority. For this to 
happen, the ICMR and National Institute of Nutrition ( NIN) needs to collaborate and 
undertake the project to devise methodology based on actual diets of Indians and 
consumption of foods along with the indicators like  population under  nutrition, child 
mortality and other related indicators . Certainly, India specific datasets will accurately  
help in  ascertaining hunger status in the country . The Committee hopes that the DHR 
would undertake this project on priority and will come up with India specific state -wise 
hunger index at the earliest.

 (Para 3.35)  
The Committee is of the considered view that ICMR must take adequate steps 
expeditiously to fill up the vacant posts at various levels in ICMR at the earliest., The 
Committee, in this connection, would lik e to be apprised of the current status of the 
recruitment process for filling up of 69 posts of Scientist „B (Non -Medical)‟, 6 posts of 
Scientist „D (Non -Medical)‟, 4 posts of Scientist „D (Dental) and 80 vacant posts of 
Assistants in the ICMR. 
 (Para 3.38)  

38 
 
The Committee desires to be apprised of the outcomes and insights of study result 
on the project entitled “Randomized Controlled Clinical study of the Ayurveda 
formulation- PJ17 for the management of Dengue fever”.  The Committee desires the 
ICMR to mak e efforts in resolving the matter of delay in sanctioning of funds with 
CCRAS, so that the project entitled “Double -blind Randomized control clinical study" for 
the "Evaluation of Ayush - GMH in the subjects of mild to moderate non -alcoholic fatty 
liver dis ease (NAFLD)” is started at the earliest. The Committee, in this connection, 
strongly recommends the ICMR, Ministry of Ayush and Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare to co -ordinate with each other to attain the objectives of projects viz. (i) 
Randomized C ontrolled Clinical study of the Ayurveda formulation - PJ17 for the 
management of Dengue fever and (ii) Double -blind Randomized control clinical study for 
the Evaluation of Ayush- GMH in the subjects of mild to moderate non-alcoholic fatty liver 
disease (NAFLD).  
 (Para 3.43)  
The Committee takes note of efforts made by ICMR towards availing research work 
opportunities in the country. The Committee is of the view that research as a career option 
is not as popular as other fields. In order to make research as a viable career opti on 
medical research must be prioritized. ICMR must engage the youth through its various 
projects/ research programmes, research in scientific endeavors so as to kindle research 
vigor amongst the youth. The Committee recommends for active engagement with pr ivate 
sector and other research institutes for advanced medical research. Such collaborations 
will promote focused research particularly on development of new drugs/vaccines, medical 
technology and devices to address emerging and evolving health issues. Th e Committee 
desires ICMR to make serious efforts to do in -depth research in the field of bio -medical 
research so that the overall health infrastructure in the country is strengthened.  
 (Para 3.50)  
The Committee expresses serious concern over the fact tha t till date, only 12 States 
have issued notifications with respect to making cancer a notifiable disease. The Committee 
believes that cancer requires exhaustive research for analysis of the disease burden to 
improve the treatment methods. With almost 18% o f the world population, and given the 
rising trend of cancer cases, our country needs to prioritize early screening, detection, 
treatment and palliative care. The Committee, therefore, strongly advocates the needs for 
declaring Cancer a "Notifiable Disease" throughout the country.

The Committee commends ICMR's decision of establishing a dedicated body in 
India Cancer Research Consortium (ICRC) to promote and prioritize cancer research in 
the country. The Committee desires to be intimated  about the developments in the three 
research projects undertaken by ICRC. Given the assessment that cancer cases is expected 
to increase by 12% in the next five years, the Committee calls upon the consortium to bring 
all relevant stakeholders viz Governme nt, policymakers, healthcare professionals and 
researchers to identify gaps that need to be bridged in cancer research in the country. The 
Committee believes that lack of funding should never come in the way of Cancer research.  
The Committee, in this rega rd, recommends DHR to chalk out a suitable scheme in 
consultation with MoH&FW to attract private investment in Cancer Research. The 
Committee further recommends DHR to assess the financial requirement for Cancer

Research and take up the requisition to the Ministry of Finance for adequate and timely 
allocation.

Sixth Report on Demands for Grants 2021-22 (Demand No. 44) of the Department of Health and 
Family Welfare (Ministry of Health & Family Welfare).

Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on

1 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.1 The Committee agrees that Nutrition, safe drinking water and clean sanitary conditions are 
fundamental in paving the way towards holistic health. The Government in encompassing all 
these parameters under the head, "Health and Well Being" has attempted to adopt the much 
needed multi-sectoral approach to hea lth. However, the Committee observes that the 137 percent 
increase in the health outlay from Rs. 94,452 crore in 2020 - 21 to Rs. 2,23,846 crore in 2021 -22 
does not compensate the inadequate funds allocated to both the Departments of Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of AYUSH. This Rs. 2,23,846 crore outlay on Health 
and Well Being includes the budget for the Department of Health and Family Welfare, 
Department of Health Research, Department of Drinking Water & Sanitation, Ministry of 
AYUSH, Package for Vaccination, Nutrition and Finance Commission(FC) Grants for Water and 
Sanitation and FC Grants for Health. Thus effectively, the budgetary allocation for health is just 
32 percent of the much hyped Rs. 2,23,846 crore funds. 
1.2 The Committee notes the observations of the Economic Survey that quotes the data from 
World Bank and WHO (Global Health Expenditure DataBase) which ranks India at 179th 
position out of 189 countries in prioritization accorded to health in its Government Budgets. The 
Committee is dismayed to note that in 2018, when the Government Health Expenditure (GHE) as 
percentage of GDP was as high as 9.27% and 9.21% in developed economies of Sweden and 
Japan, the same was just 1.4% in 2018 -19 of India. Even for developing economi es such as 
Maldives, Argentina and Colombia the GHE as % of GDP amounted to 6.65, 5.91, and 5.47 % 
respectively. 
(Para 2.8 & 2.15 of 126th Report) 
Action Taken  
1.3 The Government of India is committed to increasing health expenditure. The National 
Health Policy of 2017 is geared up towards increasing government health expenditure. The policy 
document recognizes the role of government health expenditure to ensure univ ersal health 
coverage to all. As per the NHA estimates between 2013 -14 and 2017 -18 Government health 
expenditure as a share of GDP has increased from 1.15% to 1.35%. 
 
Recommendation/Observations 
1.4 The Committee is of the view that this mismatch in alloca tion and actual expenditure is a 
sign of poor financial management and subsequently results into slashing of funds in the next 
year. The Committee understands that funds under some schemes remained unspent in view of the 
unprecedented situation due to the pandemic, however the Ministry must now take charge of the 
situation and work towards prudent budgetary allocation under different schemes. 
(Para 2.23) 
 

2 
 
Action Taken 
1.5 Due to the outbreak of COVID Pandemic some of the activities were affected and funds 
had to be reallocated to cater the emergency activities. The recommendation of the Committee is 
well taken and in view of felt need of Programme Divisions prudent budgetary allocation under 
different schemes would be done. 
 
Recommendation 
1.6 The Committee takes notes of the steps taken for strengthening the monitoring mechanism 
and simplification of referral system and issuance of guidelines for treatment of beneficiaries 
under emergent situation for effective working of the CGHS and special arrangement ma de for 
extending emergency services to the beneficiaries during PandemicCOVID -19. The Committee 
recommends the Department to give impetus to fresh measures, as per the requirement of the 
emerging situation, for upgrading the operational efficiency of CGHS so that the beneficiaries of 
CGHS get better and timely treatment. 
(Para 3.18) 
Action Taken 
1.7 The recommendations of Hon‘ble Committee have been noted. Reform measures under 
CGHS is a continuous and dynamic process. 
Recommendation 
1.8 The Committee also notes that to encourage Medical Device Industry in India and 
participate in the Government‟s “Make in India” initiative, the Institute should been couraged to 
procure equipment with CE/BIS certification. The Institute should avoid inappropriate 
procurement of medical devices/equipment with USFDA certification for basic equipment. 
However, high end equipment which is not manufactured by Indian Companies may be purchased 
from foreign manufacturers and exemption may be granted to RML hospital and such other 
hospitals/Institutes for such purchase under the "Make in India" programme. 
(Para 3.43) 
Action Taken 
1.9 As advised by the committee, the Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Medical Sciences and 
Dr. RML Hospital is already giving preferences for purchases to ―Make in India‖ initiatives. This 
hospital also encourages CE/ BIS certification to procure equipments. 
Recommendation 
 
1.10 The Committee has been given to understand that the funds allocated under BE/RE 2020 -
21 and BE 2021 -22 under Revenue and Capital for various Institutions/Organisations are 
estimated to suffice the requirement to meet the cost of establishment charges of various 
subordinate/field offices engaged in providing medical care, technical research,  vaccines/sera 
production, Drug Quality and Standards, health education and intelligence, Nursing education, 
communicable diseases. The Committee, however recommends the Department to plead for 
allocation of additional funds, if required, during 2021-22 at Restage. 
(Para 3.60) 

3 
 
Action Taken  
1.11 The Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance. 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.12 The Committee takes note that PMSSY scheme is financed through two sources, CRIF and 
GBS. PMSSY encompasses two components viz. setting up of new AIIMS and up gradation of 
Govt. Medical Colleges (GMCs). So far, setting up of 22 new AIIMS and 75 up -gradation projects 
of GMCs have been sanctioned under PMSSY. The Committee observes that keeping in view the 
past experience, there is a need to strictly monitor the execution of the PMSSY Scheme in order to 
ensure the completion of the project within the scheduled time. In order to achieve the set 
objectives, the Department also requires to have effective monitoring mechanism to cont rol the 
financial progress and to co -ordinate with the implementing agencies for ensuring timely 
implementation of the projects undertaken on setting up of new AIIMS and up -gradation of 
Government Medical Colleges (GMCs). The management of the 16 AIIMS and  GMCs must have 
Always Better Control (ABC) in order to keep the implementing agencies on the alert mode. 
 
(Para 3.69) 
Action Taken  
1.13 The Ministry has been closely monitoring the progress of PMSSY Projects in the matter of 
construction, procurement &  installation of medical equipment and recruitments of faculty and 
non-faculty personnel on a regular basis. Project monitoring and resolution of any problems in 
execution of projects happens at multiple levels.  
1.14 New AIIMS and GMC up -gradation projects in Phase III/IV onwards are being executed 
in EPC mode under which Executing Agencies (EA) are appointed for each of the Projects, who 
are empowered to take all contractual decisions. For procurement of medical equipment, HITES, 
which is a PSU of the Min istry of Health and Family Welfare, acts as the Procurement Support

vaccines indicates varying vaccine acceptance by healthcare workers who have bee n offered the

1.89 The Committee takes note of the fact that as against the global MMR decline of 45%
